E.tempting: causes identical symmetric proximal muscle weakness

nodes.text: Symmetric proximal muscle weakness with heliotrope rash or Gottron papules: suspect dermatomyositis
Measure serum creatine kinase, aldolase, and myositis-specific antibodies (anti-Mi-2, anti-Jo-1)
Obtain electromyography and muscle biopsy showing perimysial inflammation and perifascicular atrophy
Initiate high-dose systemic corticosteroids with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants
**Severe dysphagia or refractory disease:** intravenous immunoglobulin therapy
Perform routine malignancy screening due to high risk of occult cancer

periorbital purplish discoloration bilaterally

c-neuro-07-q044.boardCall: Cold water ear irrigation eliciting eye movement -> intact caloric response prevents brain death
c-neuro-07-q044.hinge: Brain death requires complete absence of all brainstem reflexes; intact slow conjugate deviation on cold caloric testing confirms persistent brainstem function.
c-neuro-07-q044.trap: Spinal reflexes (triple flexion, withdrawal) can persist in brain death, but any brainstem reflex such as caloric response precludes the diagnosis.

A.clue: Slow conjugate eye deviation during cold calorics
A.fit: Here: irrigation of ear canal with cold water results in eye movement

B.clue: Blink response to corneal touch via CN V/VII
B.fit: Not here: corneal reflex is absent, which is consistent with brain death
B.tempting: key brainstem reflex evaluated in brain death

C.clue: Pupillary constriction to direct light via CN II/III
C.fit: Not here: pupils are nonreactive, which is consistent with brain death
C.tempting: absent in clinical brain death

D.clue: Spinal cord withdrawal reflexes elicited by painful stimulation
D.fit: Not here: spinal reflexes persist in brain death and do not prevent diagnosis
D.tempting: movement on noxious stimuli is often mistaken for brain function

E.clue: Spontaneous ventilatory effort during apnea testing
E.fit: Not here: patient is not initiating spontaneous breaths above the ventilator
E.tempting: spontaneous respirations prevent brain death declaration

nodes.text: Comatose patient with catastrophic brain injury: establish prerequisite conditions
Prerequisites: normothermia, systolic blood pressure >= 100 mm Hg, rule out CNS depressants
Document coma with complete absence of motor response to painful central stimulation
Demonstrate absence of all brainstem reflexes: pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, oculovestibular, cough/gag
**Any brainstem reflex present (such as caloric response):** brain death cannot be declared
Perform apnea test: absence of spontaneous respiratory effort with elevated PaCO2
Obtain ancillary testing (cerebral angiography or EEG) if apnea testing cannot be completed

c-neuro-07-q045.boardCall: Prematurity + motor delay + spastic toe-walking + hyperreflexia -> cerebral palsy
c-neuro-07-q045.hinge: Nonprogressive upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski, toe-walking) following preterm birth and intraventricular hemorrhage define cerebral palsy.
c-neuro-07-q045.trap: Muscular dystrophy causes toe-walking and motor delay, but features proximal lower motor neuron weakness and hyporeflexia rather than spasticity and Babinski signs.

A.clue: Nonprogressive perinatal brain injury causing spastic impairment
A.fit: Here: prematurity, delayed walking, persistent Babinski signs, heel cord contractures

B.clue: Acquired autoimmune demyelinating disease of central nervous system
B.fit: Not here: congenital static encephalopathy dating back to premature birth
B.tempting: causes upper motor neuron signs and hyperreflexia

C.clue: Progressive muscle degeneration with pseudohypertrophy and Gowers sign
C.fit: Not here: bilateral Babinski signs, hyperreflexia, and perinatal IVH history
C.tempting: causes toe walking and delayed motor milestones in young boys

D.clue: Fluctuating fatigable ocular and bulbar muscle weakness
D.fit: Not here: spasticity, persistent Babinski signs, and heel cord contractures
D.tempting: causes motor delay and generalized weakness

E.clue: Neurocutaneous disorder with cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromas
E.fit: Not here: spastic motor syndrome without characteristic cutaneous lesions
E.tempting: causes pediatric developmental and neurologic abnormalities

nodes.text: Delayed motor milestones, persistent primitive reflexes, and spastic toe-walking in preterm child
Brain MRI to identify structural injury: periventricular leukomalacia or intraventricular hemorrhage
Multidisciplinary management: physical and occupational therapy to maintain joint range of motion
**Focal limb spasticity impairing function:** intramuscular botulinum toxin injection
**Generalized severe spasticity:** oral baclofen or intrathecal baclofen pump
Surgical Achilles tendon lengthening or orthopedic tendon releases for fixed contractures
Screen for comorbid visual impairment, hearing deficits, and seizure disorders

born at 29 weeks' gestation

heel cord contractures

c-neuro-07-q046.boardCall: Fluctuating ptosis + diplopia + proximal weakness -> repetitive nerve stimulation study
c-neuro-07-q046.hinge: Fatigable ocular weakness (ptosis, diplopia) combined with proximal extremity weakness suggests myasthenia gravis, confirmed by repetitive nerve stimulation and autoantibody testing.
c-neuro-07-q046.trap: Creatine kinase and muscle biopsy evaluate primary myopathies, but fluctuating fatigable weakness with ptosis indicates a neuromuscular junction disorder.

A.clue: Assesses muscle fiber breakdown in inflammatory myopathies
A.fit: Not here: prominent ptosis and diplopia indicating neuromuscular junction disorder
A.tempting: evaluates generalized proximal extremity muscle weakness

B.clue: Emergency plasma exchange for acute myasthenic crisis
B.fit: Not here: stable outpatient without acute respiratory or bulbar compromise
B.tempting: definitive therapy for severe myasthenia gravis

C.clue: Evaluates intracranial structural or demyelinating lesions
C.fit: Not here: normal reflexes without upper motor neuron signs or sensory loss
C.tempting: evaluates diplopia and generalized motor weakness

D.clue: Histopathologic tissue diagnosis of primary muscle disease
D.fit: Not here: fluctuating ocular symptoms and normal tendon reflexes
D.tempting: used to evaluate undifferentiated proximal muscle weakness

E.clue: Demonstrates decremental motor compound action potential response
E.fit: Here: bilateral ptosis, diplopia while reading, proximal extremity weakness

nodes.text: Fluctuating fatigable ptosis, diplopia, and proximal limb weakness: suspect myasthenia gravis
Perform repetitive nerve stimulation study demonstrating decremental motor compound action potential
Send serum acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies and anti-MuSK antibodies
Obtain contrast-enhanced chest CT to evaluate for thymoma
**Confirmed generalized myasthenia gravis:** initiate oral pyridostigmine
**Myasthenic crisis with respiratory failure:** plasmapheresis or intravenous immunoglobulin
Thymectomy for thymoma or young-onset AChR-positive generalized myasthenia gravis

double vision that occurs when she reads

c-neuro-07-q047.boardCall: Prior targetoid rash + large joint mono/oligoarthritis -> Lyme arthritis
c-neuro-07-q047.hinge: Disseminated Borrelia burgdorferi infection presents weeks to months after erythema migrans with intermittent or persistent inflammatory oligoarthritis affecting large joints like the knee.
c-neuro-07-q047.trap: Sexual history tempts disseminated gonococcal infection, but prior expanding rash with central clearing (erythema migrans) confirms Lyme disease.

A.clue: Migratory polyarthralgias, tenosynovitis, and pustular dermatitis
A.fit: Not here: preceding 5-cm targetoid rash with central clearing
A.tempting: sexually active with multiple inconsistent condom partners

B.clue: Negatively birefringent needle-shaped urate crystals in joint
B.fit: Not here: antecedent erythema migrans rash and oligoarticular distribution
B.tempting: causes acute inflammatory monoarthritis of knee

C.clue: Borrelia burgdorferi infection following tick-borne erythema migrans
C.fit: Here: right knee effusion weeks after 5-cm rash with central clearing

D.clue: Non-inflammatory mechanical joint degeneration with osteophytes
D.fit: Not here: 37-year-old with acute joint effusion following constitutional illness
D.tempting: causes knee and hip pain

E.clue: Symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis of small joints
E.fit: Not here: asymmetric large-joint oligoarthritis preceded by erythema migrans
E.tempting: causes inflammatory synovitis and joint effusion

nodes.text: Large joint inflammatory arthritis following erythema migrans rash: suspect Lyme arthritis
Obtain two-tiered serology: serum enzyme immunoassay (ELISA) followed by Western blot confirmation
Arthrocentesis to exclude septic arthritis and crystal arthropathy: synovial fluid leukocytosis
Administer oral doxycycline or amoxicillin for 28 days
**Refractory persistent arthritis after oral regimen:** intravenous ceftriaxone for 28 days
Post-infectious Lyme arthritis management with oral NSAIDs or disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs

moderate joint effusion
sexually active with multiple partners

c-neuro-07-q048.boardCall: Severe hyperactive delirium from urosepsis with violent agitation -> haloperidol
c-neuro-07-q048.hinge: Severely agitated, combative patients with hyperactive delirium from infection who pose an immediate safety risk are managed with low-dose haloperidol while treating the underlying cause.
c-neuro-07-q048.trap: Benzodiazepines like diazepam or midazolam exacerbate non-withdrawal delirium and worsen confusion in elderly or brain-injured patients.

A.clue: Benzodiazepine that paradoxically worsens delirium
A.fit: Not here: benzodiazepines paradoxically exacerbate confusion and cognitive impairment
A.tempting: patient already takes diazepam as needed for muscle spasms

B.clue: Antipsychotic controlling acute dangerous delirium
B.fit: Here: combative uncooperative patient hitting staff in severe urosepsis

C.clue: Nonselective beta- and alpha-1 blocker for hypertension
C.fit: Not here: normal blood pressure 110/76 mm Hg, tachycardia from sepsis
C.tempting: treats sympathetic hyperactivity and tachycardia

D.clue: Benzodiazepine causing paradoxical disinhibition in delirium
D.fit: Not here: benzodiazepines prolong delirium duration and increase complications
D.tempting: rapidly sedates acutely combative patients

E.clue: Cofactor replacing thiamine deficiency in alcohol withdrawal
E.fit: Not here: patient does not drink alcohol; delirium is from urosepsis
E.tempting: used to treat acute confusion and encephalopathy

nodes.text: Acute fluctuating attention deficit and combative agitation in systemic infection: hyperactive delirium
Initiate targeted antibiotic therapy and intravenous fluid resuscitation for underlying infection
Implement environmental and nonpharmacological reorientation measures and frequent family presence
Administer low-dose haloperidol for severe agitation posing an immediate threat to patient or staff
**Prolonged QTc interval or torsades de pointes risk:** consider second-generation antipsychotic
Avoid benzodiazepines because they worsen delirium duration and increase fall risk
Discontinue antipsychotic as soon as delirium and acute combativeness resolve

uncooperative and hits anyone who touches him

c-neuro-07-q049.boardCall: AIDS with CD4 < 50 + multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions -> cerebral toxoplasmosis
c-neuro-07-q049.hinge: Toxoplasma gondii reactivation in advanced AIDS (CD4 < 100) characteristically presents with multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia and cortex.
c-neuro-07-q049.trap: Primary CNS lymphoma also causes ring-enhancing lesions in AIDS, but multiple lesions with positive toxoplasma serology favor toxoplasmosis initially.

A.clue: Basilar leptomeningitis with elevated intracranial pressure
A.fit: Not here: five ring-enhancing parenchymal lesions on contrast head CT
A.tempting: common opportunistic fungal infection in AIDS

B.clue: Periventricular subependymal enhancement, microglial nodules, retinitis
B.fit: Not here: multiple 1- to 2-cm ring-enhancing parenchymal lesions
B.tempting: causes opportunistic CNS infection when CD4 < 50

C.clue: Single periventricular ring-enhancing lesion with EBV
C.fit: Not here: five discrete peripheral ring-enhancing lesions favor toxoplasmosis
C.tempting: second most common cause of ring-enhancing lesions in AIDS

D.clue: Reactivation of protozoan cyst causing brain lesions
D.fit: Here: AIDS patient with CD4 25/mm3 and five ring-enhancing brain lesions

E.clue: Basilar meningeal enhancement, tuberculomas, infarctions
E.fit: Not here: multiple classic ring-enhancing lesions with oral thrush
E.tempting: causes ring-enhancing tuberculomas in immunocompromised

nodes.text: Advanced AIDS (CD4 < 100) with headache and multiple ring-enhancing lesions on neuroimaging
Check serum Toxoplasma IgG antibody and send CSF for EBV PCR and Toxoplasma PCR
Initiate empiric pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin for suspected cerebral toxoplasmosis
**Clinical or radiologic improvement on repeat MRI in 10 to 14 days:** continue treatment for 6 weeks
**Lesions enlarge or fail to improve after 2 weeks:** stereotactic brain biopsy for CNS lymphoma
Initiate secondary prophylaxis with sulfadiazine plus pyrimethamine until CD4 count > 200
Optimize antiretroviral therapy once acute CNS infection is stabilized

c-neuro-07-q050.boardCall: Acute mechanical low back strain without red flags -> oral ibuprofen
c-neuro-07-q050.hinge: Acute low back pain with radicular symptoms and preserved motor/sensory function without red flags is treated with NSAIDs and maintaining regular activity.
c-neuro-07-q050.trap: Radiation to posterior thigh tempts urgent MRI or prolonged bed rest, but absence of neurologic deficits warrants conservative therapy first.

A.clue: Strict recumbency promoting deconditioning and delayed recovery
A.fit: Not here: prolonged bed rest worsens back pain and prolongs disability
A.tempting: instinctive response to severe acute back pain

B.clue: Plain radiographs evaluating fracture, spondylolisthesis, or malignancy
B.fit: Not here: young patient with acute lifting strain and no red flags
B.tempting: frequently ordered for acute traumatic back pain

C.clue: Cross-sectional imaging evaluating disc herniation or compression
C.fit: Not here: no progressive neurologic deficits, saddle anesthesia, or bowel dysfunction
C.tempting: radiation to posterior thigh suggests lumbar disc herniation

D.clue: First-line oral anti-inflammatory analgesia for acute strain
D.fit: Here: acute post-lifting back pain with normal neurologic examination

E.clue: Electrophysiologic assessment of peripheral lumbosacral radiculopathy
E.fit: Not here: normal strength and sensation, acute 2-day duration
E.tempting: evaluates radicular pain radiating into leg

nodes.text: Acute mechanical low back pain following lifting exertion: screen for red flag features
Red flags: cauda equina syndrome, progressive motor deficit, history of cancer, fever
**Red flags present (saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder incontinence):** emergent lumbar MRI
Initiate first-line conservative therapy with oral ibuprofen or naproxen
Encourage early mobilization and maintaining normal daily activities as tolerated
Avoid strict bed rest because it delays functional recovery and increases chronic disability
**Persistent disabling symptoms beyond 4 to 6 weeks:** obtain lumbar spine MRI

acute-agitation.name: Acute agitation
acute-agitation.scope: Verbal de-escalation, physical restraints, chemical restraints, intramuscular antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, QTc prolongation, medical workup
acute-agitation.core: Agitation is a symptom: protect immediate safety, use the least restrictive calming approach and search for a reversible medical cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Intoxication/withdrawal, psychosis, mania, delirium, dementia, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, pain
Recent medication change, infection, head trauma or inability to communicate needs

rows.label: Clues
items: Fluctuating attention/disorientation → delirium; hallucinations with intact attention can reflect primary psychosis
Diaphoresis, mydriasis, hypertension → stimulant intoxication; tremor/autonomic activation → withdrawal
Hyperthermia, rigidity, clonus, severe headache or focal deficit → toxic/neurologic emergency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Altered arousal and threat processing amplify behavior; sympathetic activation can worsen physiologic instability
Sedatives reduce motor activity but can conceal deterioration and impair ventilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Immediate **vital signs, pulse oximetry and fingerstick glucose**; assess trauma and toxidromes
Collateral history, medication list, focused neurologic/physical examination; assess attention and orientation
Target CBC, electrolytes, renal function, pregnancy/toxicology tests to findings; ECG before QT-prolonging drugs if feasible
Head CT for trauma, focal findings or unexplained altered mental status; never delay urgent stabilization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Verbal de-escalation**: quiet space, one speaker, personal space, simple choices; offer oral drugs
★ Psychosis/mania → **olanzapine or haloperidol**; IM route for immediate danger when oral impossible
Stimulant intoxication or alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal → **lorazepam**; respiratory monitoring
Avoid benzodiazepines in most delirium/depressant intoxication; **no IM olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepines**
★ Imminent harm → brief physical restraints, continuous monitoring, frequent reassessment; remove promptly

rows.label: Complications
items: Hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, aspiration, sudden deterioration; positional restraint can cause asphyxia
Antipsychotics → QT prolongation, dystonia/NMS; benzodiazepines → respiratory depression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Address pain, hunger, sensory impairment; reduce stimulation and preserve sleep
Use trauma-informed communication, staff training and individualized crisis plans

rows.label: Mimics
items: Akathisia: medication-linked inner restlessness; escalating antipsychotics worsens symptoms
Catatonia: posturing, negativism or stereotypy; lorazepam-responsive syndrome

acute-agitation.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency psychiatry and restraint principles.

alcohol-withdrawal.name: Alcohol withdrawal
alcohol-withdrawal.core: Autonomic and neuropsychiatric excitation after reducing prolonged heavy alcohol intake; progression from mild symptoms to life-threatening delirium.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior withdrawal seizures/delirium, repeated detoxifications, heavy sustained use, older age
Acute illness, electrolyte depletion, concurrent sedative dependence; poor support increases outpatient failure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, insomnia, nausea; symptoms possible with **positive blood alcohol**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Chronic ethanol → downregulated GABA inhibition/upregulated NMDA excitation; cessation unmasks neuronal hyperactivity
Repeated episodes → kindling, progressively lower seizure threshold

rows.label: Dx
items: **Clinical diagnosis** + time since reduction; bedside glucose, CBC, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate, liver tests
★ **CIWA-Ar** if communicative; ≥19 severe; delirium/intubation → **RASS/MINDS**
First/focal seizure, head injury, focal deficit, atypical timing → head CT; do not assume withdrawal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Diazepam/chlordiazepoxide** symptom-triggered; liver dysfunction/older frail adults → **lorazepam/oxazepam**
★ Seizures/delirium → monitored inpatient **IV benzodiazepines**; refractory → ICU phenobarbital with respiratory monitoring
★ **Parenteral thiamine**; hypoglycemia → immediate dextrose, never wait; correct electrolyte deficits
Phenytoin ineffective; antipsychotics/clonidine/dexmedetomidine adjuncts only, without seizure protection

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, dysrhythmias, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis; excessive sedation → respiratory depression
Malnutrition → Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; suspected → high-dose IV thiamine

rows.label: Prevention
items: High-risk inpatients → preventive benzodiazepines; outpatient withdrawal only if mild, reliable supervision
Recovery: **naltrexone** unless opioids/acute hepatitis; **acamprosate** unless severe CKD; addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatic encephalopathy: asterixis, decompensated cirrhosis, less autonomic excitation
Sepsis: infectious source, hypotension, persistent inflammatory findings
Sedative withdrawal: benzodiazepine/barbiturate reduction; similar syndrome, different exposure

bone-tumors.name: Bone tumors
bone-tumors.scope: Osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, chondrosarcoma, giant cell tumor of bone, osteochondroma, osteoid osteoma, bone metastases, biopsy
bone-tumors.core: Persistent focal bone pain, a growing mass, or a destructive radiographic lesion requires planned evaluation before biopsy or fixation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Osteosarcoma: adolescence, prior radiation, Paget disease; chondrosarcoma: older adults
Hereditary multiple exostoses predispose to osteochondromas; most adult malignant bone lesions are metastases

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Night/rest pain**, enlarging mass, constitutional symptoms or pathologic fracture → concerning lesion
Osteoid osteoma: nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs; small cortical nidus
Osteochondroma: painless metaphyseal exostosis with medullary continuity; new growth after maturity concerning

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor lineage determines osteoid, cartilage or primitive-cell production; aggressive growth destroys cortex
Giant cell tumor: neoplastic stromal cells recruit osteoclast-like giant cells, causing locally aggressive osteolysis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Plain radiographs first**; assess location, margins, periosteal reaction and matrix
Aggressive lesion → MRI entire involved bone/adjacent joint; chest CT for lung metastases
★ **Orthopedic oncology plans biopsy tract**; core biopsy after imaging, before definitive treatment
CBC, ESR/CRP if infection suspected; normal labs do not exclude malignancy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Osteosarcoma → **neoadjuvant chemotherapy + wide resection**, then postoperative chemotherapy
Ewing → systemic chemotherapy plus surgery and/or radiation
Chondrosarcoma → wide surgical excision; conventional tumors relatively chemo/radioresistant
Symptomatic osteoid osteoma → radiofrequency ablation; asymptomatic osteochondroma → observation
Giant cell tumor → curettage/reconstruction; selected unresectable lesions → denosumab

rows.label: Complications
items: Pathologic fracture, neurovascular compromise, pulmonary metastases; limb surgery and chemotherapy morbidity

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: infection markers, cultures; may closely resemble Ewing
Bone metastases: older adult, multiple lesions; myeloma: anemia, monoclonal protein

bone-tumors.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

brachial-plexus-disorders.name: Brachial plexus disorders
brachial-plexus-disorders.scope: Erb palsy (upper trunk C5-C6), Klumpke palsy (lower trunk C8-T1), thoracic outlet syndrome, radiation-induced brachial plexopathy, neoplastic infiltration (Pancoast tumor), neuralgic amyotrophy
brachial-plexus-disorders.core: Weakness and sensory loss spanning several peripheral nerves in one arm suggest a plexus lesion rather than isolated mononeuropathy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Shoulder dystocia, traction injuries, motorcycle crashes; prior breast/axillary radiation
Apical lung tumor, cervical rib, repetitive overhead activity; neuralgic amyotrophy often postinfectious

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Severe shoulder pain followed by weakness** days later → neuralgic amyotrophy
Thoracic outlet: positional lower-plexus symptoms; swelling/cyanosis suggests venous compression
★ Progressive painful lower-trunk deficit plus **Horner syndrome** → Pancoast tumor

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Plexus traction, compression, inflammatory injury, or tumor infiltration disrupts multiple terminal nerves

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **EMG/nerve conduction studies** localize affected trunks; sensory responses reduced, paraspinals usually spared
MRI brachial plexus for structural lesion; chest imaging for lower-trunk symptoms or cancer concern
Vascular thoracic outlet symptoms → duplex ultrasound, CT/MR angiography; provocative maneuvers alone insufficient
★ New deficit after radiation → **exclude recurrent cancer** before attributing to radiation injury

rows.label: Tx
items: Birth traction palsy: range-of-motion rehabilitation; persistent severe deficits → specialist nerve-repair evaluation
Neuralgic amyotrophy: analgesia, physical/occupational therapy; consider early corticosteroids for pain
Neurogenic thoracic outlet: posture modification and physical therapy; refractory objective deficits → decompression
Vascular compromise/thrombosis → urgent vascular evaluation; neoplastic plexopathy → treat malignancy

rows.label: Complications
items: Denervation atrophy, contractures, chronic neuropathic pain; venous thrombosis or distal arterial ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid prolonged traction and compressive positioning; maintain shoulder mobility during recovery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cervical radiculopathy: neck provocation, preserved sensory responses, paraspinal denervation
Rotator cuff tear: mechanical shoulder weakness without distal sensory loss

table.title: Patterns
rows: Adducted, internally rotated arm; extended elbow

brain-death.name: Brain death
brain-death.scope: Prerequisites (normothermia, normal BP), clinical exam (coma, absent brainstem reflexes), apnea test, ancillary testing (cerebral blood flow studies)
brain-death.core: Permanent loss of all brain function, including brainstem function, constitutes death; a beating heart on ventilation does not negate the diagnosis.

rows.label: Principle
items: Known catastrophic irreversible brain injury; compatible neuroimaging; adequate observation period

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Prerequisites: **temperature ≥36°C**, adult SBP ≥100 and MAP ≥75 mm Hg
Exclude paralysis/metabolic confounders; sedatives: ≥5 half-lives, longer if impaired clearance
★ Examination: **coma**, no brain-mediated motor response; absent brainstem reflexes (table)

rows.label: Don't
items: Oculocephalic testing with possible cervical injury; use caloric testing after confirming ear integrity
Declare death with any brain-mediated response or spontaneous breath
Use ancillary testing to bypass hypothermia or high CNS-depressant levels

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Spinal reflex movements may persist without contradicting diagnosis
Incomplete examination or unsafe apnea test → radionuclide cerebral perfusion or catheter angiography
After temperature ≤35.5°C, wait ≥24 hours following rewarming to ≥36°C

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Apnea test: no breaths, **PaCO2 ≥60 and ≥20 above baseline**, pH <7.30
Preoxygenate; abort apnea testing for hypotension, hypoxemia or unstable arrhythmia
★ 2023 update: **EEG no longer accepted** as ancillary testing; pediatric requirements differ

brain-tumors.name: Brain tumors
brain-tumors.scope: Metastatic brain tumors, glioblastoma, meningioma, pediatric tumors (medulloblastoma), vestibular schwannoma
brain-tumors.core: Progressive focal deficits, new seizures or headache with raised intracranial pressure require brain imaging for a mass lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known lung, breast, melanoma, renal or colorectal malignancy → brain metastases
Prior cranial radiation; NF 2 predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning headache, vomiting, papilledema; altered consciousness or pupillary asymmetry → impending herniation
Frontal lesions → personality change; motor cortex → weakness; posterior fossa → ataxia
Pediatric posterior fossa mass can obstruct CSF flow and rapidly cause hydrocephalus

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor disrupts local brain function and blood–brain barrier → vasogenic edema
Fixed cranial volume makes expanding tissue/CSF raise pressure and threaten brainstem perfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Contrast MRI brain** best defines mass, edema and multiplicity; CT for unstable patients
Metastatic pattern → search primary with chest/abdominal imaging; tissue diagnosis when needed
★ Suspected mass with pressure signs → **avoid LP** until safe after imaging
Vestibular symptoms → audiometry and MRI internal auditory canals

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic edema → **dexamethasone**; herniation → head elevation, hypertonic saline/mannitol, emergency neurosurgery
Seizure → levetiracetam; no routine antiseizure prophylaxis for every seizure-naive tumor patient
★ **Resection versus radiation** depends on lesion, symptoms, accessibility and systemic disease
Medulloblastoma → resection, chemotherapy and usually craniospinal radiation; avoid/delay radiation in very young children

rows.label: Complications
items: Obstructive hydrocephalus, herniation, hemorrhage, persistent neurologic deficits
Radiation injury, cognitive decline, steroid hyperglycemia and infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Abscess: infection context and central diffusion restriction
Primary CNS lymphoma: often periventricular; steroids can obscure biopsy
Stroke: abrupt maximal onset with vascular distribution

brain-tumors.evidence: Not checked online; established neuro-oncology teaching.

carotid-artery-stenosis.name: Carotid artery stenosis
carotid-artery-stenosis.scope: Asymptomatic carotid bruit, carotid duplex ultrasound, medical management, indications for carotid endarterectomy
carotid-artery-stenosis.core: Carotid atherosclerosis causes ipsilateral retinal or cerebral ischemia; intervention depends on symptoms, stenosis severity, and operative risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia; coronary or peripheral arterial disease
Prior neck radiation increases stenosis and surgical complexity

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Amaurosis fugax**, contralateral weakness/numbness, or aphasia → symptomatic disease
Bruit may be incidental; loudness does not measure severity, complete occlusion may be silent
Isolated dizziness or syncope rarely represents carotid-territory ischemia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Plaque rupture → artery-to-artery emboli; critical narrowing can reduce cerebral perfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected stenosis or selected incidental bruit evaluation → **carotid duplex ultrasound**
CTA/MRA confirms anatomy before intervention; brain imaging evaluates neurologic deficits
★ **No routine screening** of asymptomatic general adults; bruit auscultation is an unreliable screen

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All: **antiplatelet + high-intensity statin**, BP and diabetes control
Symptomatic operative candidates: endarterectomy generally within **2 weeks**, after neurologic stabilization
Classic asymptomatic CEA criteria: ≥70%, life expectancy ≥3–5 years, perioperative stroke/death <3%; individualized decision
CREST-2: asymptomatic stenting benefited selected patients; CEA lacked significant benefit; avoid automatic surgery
Symptomatic older adults: CEA generally preferred to stenting; high surgical-risk anatomy may favor stenting

rows.label: Complications
items: Ischemic stroke, recurrent TIAs; procedure → stroke, MI, cranial nerve injury
Post-revascularization hyperperfusion syndrome → headache, seizures, intracerebral hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, Mediterranean-style diet; sustained vascular risk reduction
New focal neurologic symptoms → emergency stroke assessment, even after symptom resolution

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic stenosis: cardiac murmur radiates to both carotids
Cardioembolism: atrial fibrillation or cardiac thrombus; multiple vascular territories
Migraine aura: gradually spreading positive visual/sensory symptoms

table.title: Symptomatic ipsilateral stenosis
rows: Selected patients: age, sex, comorbidity matter

carpal-tunnel-syndrome.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
carpal-tunnel-syndrome.scope: Median nerve entrapment, pregnancy and endocrine risk factors, Phalen and Tinel tests, wrist splinting, corticosteroid injection, surgical release
carpal-tunnel-syndrome.core: Median nerve compression at the wrist causes nocturnal paresthesias in the thumb, index, middle, and radial ring fingers.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pregnancy/fluid retention, obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis
Forceful repetitive hand activity, wrist trauma; dialysis-associated amyloid in selected patients

rows.label: Clues
items: Shaking hand relieves symptoms; driving or sustained wrist flexion aggravates symptoms
★ **Thenar weakness/atrophy**, dropping objects, impaired thumb opposition → advanced nerve injury
Central palm sensation usually spared because palmar cutaneous branch bypasses tunnel
Bilateral symptoms common; isolated little-finger symptoms argue against median neuropathy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Raised pressure beneath transverse carpal ligament → median nerve ischemia/demyelination
Long-standing compression progresses to axonal loss and persistent motor impairment

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical history + **Phalen/Tinel or carpal compression** findings support clinical diagnosis
Phalen: sustained wrist flexion; Tinel: percussion over median nerve reproduces distal paresthesia
★ **Nerve-conduction studies/EMG** for atypical presentation, severity assessment, or uncertain diagnosis before surgery
Targeted TSH/glucose testing when systemic disease suspected; routine wrist imaging unnecessary

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Mild/moderate → **neutral-position wrist splint at night**, ergonomic modification
Local corticosteroid injection for persistent symptoms or short-term relief; pregnancy often resolves postpartum
★ Severe deficit, denervation, or failed conservative care → **surgical carpal tunnel release**
NSAIDs do not relieve the underlying compression; avoid repeated ineffective analgesic-only management

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent sensory loss and thenar wasting if severe compression persists
Injection → transient hyperglycemia, rare nerve injury; surgery → scar pain or incomplete release

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reduce prolonged wrist flexion/extension and forceful vibration; adjust workstation and tools
Manage contributing endocrine/inflammatory disease; reassess worsening motor function promptly

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cervical radiculopathy: neck pain, dermatomal weakness/reflex changes
Ulnar neuropathy: little finger/ulnar ring symptoms, interosseous weakness
Pronator syndrome: proximal forearm pain with palmar sensory involvement

carpal-tunnel-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established peripheral nerve localization and management.

cerebellar-disorders.name: Cerebellar disorders
cerebellar-disorders.scope: Acute cerebellar ataxia, cerebellar signs, toxic cerebellar degeneration (cytarabine, phenytoin, alcohol), paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, Friedreich ataxia, imaging
cerebellar-disorders.core: Dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor, and a broad-based gait localize dysfunction to the cerebellum or its connections.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent viral infection in children; chronic alcohol exposure or malnutrition
Phenytoin toxicity, high-dose cytarabine, occult malignancy; inherited recessive disease

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Abrupt ataxia with **headache, vomiting, focal deficits** → posterior circulation emergency
Midline lesions: truncal instability; hemispheric lesions: ipsilateral limb incoordination
Scanning dysarthria, gaze-evoked nystagmus; imbalance persists with eyes open

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impaired timing and error correction; lateral cerebellum coordinates ipsilateral extremities
Alcohol predominantly damages anterior vermis; paraneoplastic disease causes immune-mediated Purkinje cell loss

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Acute focal or persistent unexplained ataxia → **brain MRI**, especially posterior fossa
CT first if hemorrhage suspected; negative CT does not exclude cerebellar infarction
Check glucose, toxic exposures, phenytoin level; consider B12, thyroid testing
Subacute progressive course → paraneoplastic antibodies and malignancy search; hereditary pattern → genetic testing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected nutritional deficiency → **IV thiamine** promptly; give glucose immediately if hypoglycemic
★ Toxic **cytarabine/phenytoin** → stop culprit; cytarabine toxicity requires urgent oncology review
Postinfectious acute cerebellar ataxia: observation/support after exclusion of dangerous causes
Paraneoplastic syndrome: treat tumor, consider immunotherapy; rehabilitation for all persistent deficits

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration; cerebellar infarction/edema → obstructive hydrocephalus and herniation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Alcohol cessation, nutritional repletion; review anticonvulsant levels and interactions

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sensory ataxia: impaired proprioception, marked worsening with eye closure
Vestibular disease: vertigo predominates, no limb dysmetria

table.title: Progressive syndromes
rows: GAA expansion; areflexia, extensor plantars, cardiomyopathy
Weeks–months; breast/ovarian or small-cell lung cancer

cerebellar-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established neurologic localization and toxicology teaching.

cerebral-palsy.name: Cerebral palsy
cerebral-palsy.scope: Spastic diplegia, spastic hemiplegia, spastic quadriplegia, dyskinetic (athetoid) cerebral palsy, ataxic, prematurity and intraventricular hemorrhage risk, hyperreflexia, contractures, multidisciplinary management
cerebral-palsy.core: Persistent abnormal posture and movement from a nonprogressive injury to the developing brain; functional manifestations change with growth.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prematurity, periventricular leukomalacia, intraventricular hemorrhage, perinatal stroke
Congenital infection, brain malformation, neonatal hypoxic-ischemic injury, kernicterus

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Delayed motor milestones**, persistent primitive reflexes, abnormal tone; early hand preference suggests hemiplegia
Spasticity: velocity-dependent tone, hyperreflexia, clonus, extensor plantar responses
Feeding difficulty, drooling, asymmetric posture; cognition may be normal

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immature motor pathways injured before, during, or shortly after birth; injury itself remains static

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical developmental/neurologic assessment**; brain MRI defines injury pattern or malformation
Assess hearing, vision, communication, nutrition, epilepsy, and intellectual function
Loss of acquired skills or progressive weakness → metabolic/genetic evaluation rather than presumed cerebral palsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Early multidisciplinary rehabilitation**: physical, occupational, speech and feeding support
Focal spasticity → botulinum toxin; generalized troublesome spasticity → oral baclofen
Severe refractory spasticity → intrathecal baclofen or selected dorsal rhizotomy
Orthoses, mobility aids; fixed contractures/hip displacement → orthopedic evaluation
Treat seizures; swallowing assessment and enteral feeding when aspiration or inadequate intake

rows.label: Complications
items: Contractures, hip subluxation, scoliosis, pain, osteoporosis; aspiration, malnutrition, epilepsy
Musculoskeletal deformities can progress despite static brain lesion

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Antenatal magnesium sulfate** for imminent early preterm birth reduces cerebral palsy risk
Treat severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia; therapeutic hypothermia for eligible neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
Hip surveillance, stretching, adequate nutrition reduce secondary disability

rows.label: Mimics
items: Muscular dystrophy: progressive proximal weakness, elevated CK
Dopa-responsive dystonia: diurnal fluctuation, marked levodopa response

cerebral-palsy.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric neurology and perinatal prevention teaching.

cervical-radiculopathy.name: Cervical radiculopathy
cervical-radiculopathy.scope: C5-C8 radiculopathy, cervical disc herniation, cervical spondylotic myelopathy, LMN arm and UMN leg signs, Spurling test, conservative management, MRI cervical spine, surgical decompression
cervical-radiculopathy.core: Neck pain radiating down one arm with a dermatomal sensory deficit and reduced corresponding reflex.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Disc herniation in younger adults; osteophytes and foraminal narrowing with aging
Repetitive neck loading, smoking, prior cervical injury

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Spurling test**: extension, ipsilateral rotation, axial compression reproduce arm symptoms
Shoulder abduction may relieve root pain
★ **Myelopathy**: hand clumsiness, gait imbalance, LMN arms plus UMN legs; late bladder dysfunction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Root compression → segmental weakness; central canal stenosis → spinal cord dysfunction

rows.label: Dx
items: Map strength, sensation, reflexes; examine gait, plantar responses, Hoffmann sign
★ **Cervical MRI**: myelopathy, progressive deficit, cancer/infection concern, or failed conservative care
EMG/nerve conduction studies if localization uncertain; sensory responses usually preserved in radiculopathy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated: **NSAIDs + physical therapy**, activity modification; most improve within weeks
Persistent disabling root pain → consider epidural steroid injection or surgical referral
Cord compression or progressive motor deficit → urgent spine evaluation for decompression
Avoid cervical manipulation with suspected myelopathy

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent denervation and muscle atrophy; untreated cord compression → irreversible disability

rows.label: Prevention
items: Ergonomic adjustments, neck strengthening, smoking cessation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Carpal tunnel: median hand symptoms, positive Phalen, no neck provocation
Rotator cuff disease: painful shoulder motion, preserved distal neurologic examination
Brachial plexopathy: multiple roots/nerves, abnormal sensory nerve responses

cirrhosis-and-portal-hypertension.name: Cirrhosis and portal hypertension
cirrhosis-and-portal-hypertension.scope: Ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatic encephalopathy, esophageal varices, hepatorenal syndrome, hepatocellular carcinoma screening
cirrhosis-and-portal-hypertension.core: Cirrhosis produces portal hypertension and synthetic failure; new ascites, bleeding, confusion or kidney injury signals decompensation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Alcohol, chronic HBV/HCV, metabolic steatotic liver disease; autoimmune/cholestatic disorders

rows.label: Clues
items: Splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, spider angiomas, jaundice, muscle wasting
Encephalopathy triggers: GI bleeding, infection, constipation, sedatives, hypokalemia
SBP may present only with subtle confusion or renal deterioration; fever/pain can be absent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fibrosis raises intrahepatic resistance; splanchnic vasodilation lowers effective arterial volume
Portal collaterals bleed; impaired toxin clearance causes neuropsychiatric dysfunction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ New/worsening or hospitalized ascites → **diagnostic paracentesis**; PMN **≥250/µL** → treat SBP
SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL supports portal hypertension; send ascitic culture in bedside blood-culture bottles
HRS-AKI: exclude shock, nephrotoxins, obstruction and structural injury; assess volume response
MELD-Na/MELD 3.0 guides prognosis/transplant assessment; ammonia does not establish encephalopathy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Variceal bleed → resuscitate, **octreotide + ceftriaxone**, urgent endoscopic banding; refractory → TIPS
Ascites → sodium restriction, spironolactone ± furosemide; tense ascites → paracentesis, albumin if >5 L
★ SBP → **ceftriaxone**, albumin for high-risk renal/liver dysfunction; reassess response
Encephalopathy → lactulose to 2–3 soft stools/day; recurrent episodes → add rifaximin; correct trigger
HRS → stop diuretics/nephrotoxins, **terlipressin + albumin** after volume assessment; monitor hypoxia; transplant evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: HCC, recurrent infection, malnutrition, hepatopulmonary syndrome; TIPS can worsen encephalopathy
Avoid NSAIDs, sedatives and unnecessary fluid loading; INR alone poorly predicts procedural bleeding

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Ultrasound + AFP every 6 months** for HCC surveillance in eligible cirrhosis
Carvedilol for clinically significant portal hypertension when tolerated; banding if indicated and beta blocker unsuitable
After SBP → antibiotic prophylaxis; alcohol abstinence, hepatitis vaccines, adequate protein intake

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cardiac ascites: high SAAG with ascitic protein ≥2.5 g/dL
Malignant/TB ascites: usually low SAAG

cranial-nerve-palsies.name: Cranial nerve palsies
cranial-nerve-palsies.scope: CN III palsy, CN IV palsy, CN VI palsy, Bell palsy (CN VII, hyperacusis, corticosteroids), microvascular diabetic neuropathy, cavernous sinus thrombosis
cranial-nerve-palsies.core: Localize diplopia by the weak extraocular muscle; distinguish peripheral facial paralysis from a central lesion by forehead involvement.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, hypertension → ischemic mononeuropathy; trauma → trochlear injury
Sinusitis or facial infection → cavernous sinus thrombosis; pregnancy associated with Bell palsy

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Multiple ocular palsies + fever, proptosis, chemosis** → cavernous sinus thrombosis
Bell palsy: unilateral upper/lower facial weakness, altered taste, hyperacusis; no other focal deficits
Raised ICP may produce unilateral or bilateral abducens palsy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Diabetic ischemia often spares superficial parasympathetic CN III fibers; compression threatens pupil function
CN VII inflammation within facial canal disrupts facial movement and stapedius innervation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Acute CN III palsy → urgent **CTA/MRA**, especially painful or pupil-involving; exclude aneurysm
Typical isolated Bell palsy: clinical; atypical/recurrent palsy → MRI, targeted Lyme testing
Suspected cavernous thrombosis → contrast MRI/MRV or CT venography; blood cultures

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Bell palsy within 72 hours → **prednisone**; add valacyclovir for severe paralysis
★ Artificial tears, nighttime ointment and eyelid taping to protect exposed cornea
Cavernous thrombosis: IV vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole; source drainage, consider anticoagulation
Microvascular palsy: vascular risk control, temporary patch/prism; reassess if persistent or progressive

rows.label: Complications
items: Exposure keratitis, corneal ulceration; facial synkinesis after recovery
Septic thrombosis → meningitis, stroke, blindness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat facial/sinus infections; optimize diabetes and BP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Stroke: forehead relatively spared with contralateral limb findings
Myasthenia: fatigable variable weakness, normal pupils
Ramsay Hunt: ear vesicles and otalgia with facial paralysis

table.title: Ocular localization
rows: Worse downstairs; compensatory opposite head tilt

cranial-nerve-palsies.evidence: Not checked online; established neuro-ophthalmology and Bell palsy teaching.

encephalitis.name: Encephalitis
encephalitis.scope: Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1), temporal lobe lesions, CSF analysis (elevated RBCs, lymphocytic pleocytosis, PCR), IV acyclovir, West Nile virus, autoimmune encephalitis
encephalitis.core: Fever with sustained altered mental status, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits suggests brain inflammation and warrants immediate empiric acyclovir.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: HSV-1 often occurs without immunosuppression; mosquito exposure suggests arboviruses
Autoimmune disease or tumor association; anti-NMDA receptor disease sometimes accompanies ovarian teratoma

rows.label: Clues
items: HSV: personality change, aphasia, olfactory hallucinations, focal seizures
★ **Temporal lobe abnormalities** strongly suggest HSV; hemorrhagic CSF possible but not required
West Nile: movement disorder or asymmetric flaccid weakness; anti-NMDA: psychosis, dyskinesia, autonomic instability
Reduced consciousness, status epilepticus, or respiratory compromise → ICU-level care

rows.label: Pathophys
items: HSV causes necrotizing inflammation, often limbic/temporal; mosquito-borne viruses infect neuronal tissue
Autoantibodies against neuronal surface antigens disrupt synaptic signaling

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **LP: CSF cells, protein, glucose, HSV PCR**; lymphocytes, ↑protein, usually normal glucose
Neuroimaging before LP for focal deficits, papilledema, marked impaired consciousness, or suspected mass effect
MRI more sensitive than CT; EEG identifies nonconvulsive seizures or temporal periodic discharges
Early negative PCR with strong suspicion → continue treatment and repeat CSF PCR in 3–7 days
West Nile: CSF IgM; autoimmune suspicion → CSF/serum antibodies and tumor search

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected HSV → **IV acyclovir immediately**, usually 14–21 days; do not await PCR
Airway/seizure support; possible bacterial infection → ceftriaxone + vancomycin; Listeria risk → add ampicillin
Acyclovir: renal adjustment, IV hydration; West Nile: supportive care
★ Autoimmune disease → **steroids, IVIG/plasma exchange**, tumor removal after infectious evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent memory impairment, epilepsy, focal deficits, death; acyclovir crystal nephropathy
Severe autoimmune disease: arrhythmia, hypoventilation, prolonged rehabilitation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Mosquito repellent, protective clothing, vector control; no routine HSV encephalitis vaccine

rows.label: Mimics
items: Bacterial meningitis: neutrophilic CSF, low glucose; overlap requires empiric coverage
Toxic/metabolic delirium: systemic explanation without inflammatory CSF
Primary psychosis: lacks new seizures, dysautonomia, or focal neurologic abnormalities

encephalitis.evidence: Not checked online; established infectious and autoimmune neurology teaching.

epilepsy.name: Epilepsy
epilepsy.scope: Focal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, absence seizures, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, EEG findings, antiepileptic therapy (valproate, levetiracetam, lamotrigine), lifestyle counseling
epilepsy.core: Recurrent unprovoked seizures reflect epilepsy; classify focal versus generalized onset before choosing a maintenance antiseizure drug.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior brain injury, stroke, CNS infection, developmental lesions, genetic predisposition
Sleep deprivation, alcohol withdrawal and missed drugs can precipitate seizures; provoked seizures alone ≠ epilepsy

rows.label: Clues
items: Focal onset: aura, unilateral motor activity, automatisms or impaired awareness; may evolve bilaterally
Generalized tonic-clonic: abrupt loss of consciousness, stiffening/jerking, postictal confusion, lateral tongue injury
Absence: staring, immediate recovery; JME: morning myoclonus ± generalized convulsions

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormally synchronized cortical neuronal discharges impair awareness, sensation or motor function
Excitatory/inhibitory imbalance may arise from structural lesions or inherited channel/network dysfunction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **EEG and epilepsy-protocol MRI** after unprovoked seizure; normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy
Epilepsy: ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24 hours apart, or one with high recurrence risk/defined syndrome
Check glucose/electrolytes and provoking causes; urgent CT for trauma, focal deficit or persistent altered consciousness
Absence: generalized **3-Hz spike-wave**, provoked by hyperventilation; JME: generalized polyspike-wave

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Convulsion **≥5 minutes** → airway/glucose, **lorazepam**, then IV levetiracetam/fosphenytoin/valproate
Focal epilepsy → lamotrigine or levetiracetam; generalized tonic-clonic/JME → broad-spectrum agent
★ Valproate effective for generalized syndromes; **avoid when pregnancy possible** if alternatives effective
Pure absence → ethosuximide; absence plus generalized tonic-clonic → broad-spectrum drug
Avoid carbamazepine/phenytoin for absence/myoclonic syndromes; drug-resistant focal disease → surgical evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Status epilepticus, injury, aspiration, SUDEP; valproate → hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, teratogenicity
Lamotrigine → serious rash with rapid titration; levetiracetam → irritability/mood symptoms

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adherence, regular sleep, avoid alcohol excess; no abrupt drug withdrawal
Driving restrictions follow local law; no unsupervised swimming/heights; preconception folate and drug review

rows.label: Mimics
items: Syncope: prodrome, rapid recovery; brief jerks possible
Psychogenic nonepileptic events: video-EEG confirms typical event without epileptic correlate

epilepsy.evidence: Pregnancy recommendations checked 2026-10-30: [AAN/AES/SMFM 2024](https://www.aan.com/PressRoom/Home/PressRelease/5170); classification established teaching.

giant-cell-arteritis.name: Giant cell arteritis
giant-cell-arteritis.scope: Giant cell arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, vision loss
giant-cell-arteritis.core: New headache with jaw claudication or visual symptoms after age 50 requires immediate glucocorticoids to prevent irreversible blindness.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, female sex, Northern European ancestry; frequently overlaps polymyalgia rheumatica
Age <50 makes this diagnosis very unlikely

rows.label: Clues
items: Scalp tenderness, abnormal temporal artery, fever, weight loss, fatigue
★ **Transient monocular loss, diplopia, or sudden painless visual loss** → ocular ischemia
PMR: bilateral shoulder/hip aching, morning stiffness >45 minutes; true muscle strength preserved

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Granulomatous inflammation of large/medium arteries → intimal proliferation and ischemic narrowing
Posterior ciliary artery involvement causes arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ESR/CRP and CBC**: inflammation, thrombocytosis, normocytic anemia support; normal markers do not fully exclude
★ **Temporal artery biopsy** confirms; skip lesions can cause false negative, so obtain adequate segment
Ultrasound halo sign useful in experienced centers; arrange testing promptly after treatment begins
Assess pulses, arm pressures, bruits; CTA/MRA for suspected aortic/branch-vessel involvement
PMR: elevated inflammatory markers, normal CK; screen all PMR patients for cranial/visual symptoms

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected cranial GCA → **high-dose oral prednisone now**, before biopsy
★ Threatened or established visual loss → **IV methylprednisolone** urgently; ophthalmology consultation
Taper slowly with symptom/marker monitoring; tocilizumab can reduce steroid exposure in selected patients
Isolated PMR → lower-dose prednisone; failure to improve promptly → reconsider diagnosis

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent blindness, often sequential fellow-eye involvement; stroke, aortic aneurysm/dissection
Prolonged steroids → infection, diabetes, cataracts, osteoporosis; IL-6 blockade can suppress inflammatory markers

rows.label: Prevention
items: Bone protection and fracture-risk assessment during prolonged steroids; monitor BP/glucose
Educate about recurrent visual symptoms, jaw pain, limb claudication; evaluate aorta over time

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonarteritic ischemic optic neuropathy: vascular risks, no systemic inflammatory syndrome
Myositis: objective proximal weakness, elevated CK
TMJ disease: local joint pain/clicking rather than chewing-induced ischemic fatigue

giant-cell-arteritis.evidence: Not checked online; established rheumatologic emergency and PMR management.

guillain-barre-syndrome.name: Guillain-Barré syndrome
guillain-barre-syndrome.scope: Ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis, hyporeflexia, autonomic instability, preceding infection (Campylobacter jejuni), albuminocytologic dissociation, IVIG or plasma exchange
guillain-barre-syndrome.core: Rapidly progressive symmetric weakness with reduced reflexes after infection suggests immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy; respiratory and autonomic monitoring are immediate priorities.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Campylobacter gastroenteritis, respiratory viral infection, CMV; typically 1–3 weeks earlier
Rare postvaccination association; infection poses greater risk than routine vaccination

rows.label: Clues
items: Leg weakness ascends over days, paresthesias, back/radicular pain, bilateral facial weakness
★ **Areflexia with flaccid weakness**; sensory complaints usually exceed objective sensory loss
★ **BP swings, arrhythmias, urinary retention**, bulbar dysfunction indicate severe disease
Miller Fisher variant: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia; maximal weakness usually within 4 weeks

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Molecular mimicry triggers antibodies against peripheral nerve components
Demyelinating conduction block most common in US; axonal variants also occur

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serial **forced vital capacity and inspiratory force**; pulse oximetry misses early ventilatory weakness
LP: **↑protein with few cells**; CSF may be normal during first week
Nerve conduction studies: slowing/conduction block or axonal loss; normal early studies do not exclude
Marked CSF pleocytosis, sensory level, or early sphincter dysfunction → reconsider mimics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Admit for telemetry, swallowing evaluation, frequent strength and breathing assessments
Declining FVC, often <20 mL/kg, weak cough/bulbar dysfunction → **early elective intubation**
★ **IVIG or plasma exchange** for nonambulatory, rapidly progressive, or significant respiratory/bulbar disease
Do not combine routinely; **glucocorticoids do not help**
DVT prophylaxis, pressure care, nutrition, pain control, PT; avoid succinylcholine because hyperkalemia risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, aspiration, lethal dysautonomia, VTE, pressure injuries
Residual weakness, neuropathic pain, prolonged fatigue; recovery usually spans months

rows.label: Prevention
items: No established primary prophylaxis; early rehabilitation and immobilization precautions reduce secondary injury
Monitor for treatment-related fluctuations; progression beyond 8 weeks raises concern for CIDP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Transverse myelitis: sensory level, early bladder dysfunction, eventual hyperreflexia
Myasthenia gravis: fatigable ocular/bulbar weakness, normal reflexes and sensation
Botulism: descending paralysis, pupillary dysfunction, preserved sensorium

guillain-barre-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established neurology teaching.

herpes-zoster.name: Herpes zoster
herpes-zoster.scope: Varicella zoster reactivation, dermatomal rash, herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Ramsay Hunt syndrome, oral antivirals, postherpetic neuralgia, Shingrix vaccine
herpes-zoster.core: Latent varicella-zoster reactivation causes painful unilateral dermatomal vesicles; ophthalmic involvement or disseminated disease changes urgency and treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, HIV, malignancy, transplantation, immunosuppressive drugs
Previous chickenpox or live varicella vaccination establishes latency; no new exposure required

rows.label: Clues
items: Burning/allodynia can precede eruption by days; crops crust over approximately 7–10 days
★ **V1 distribution, nasal-tip lesions, eye pain** → urgent ophthalmology for zoster ophthalmicus
★ **Ear vesicles + ipsilateral facial paralysis** ± hearing/vestibular symptoms → Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Multiple noncontiguous dermatomes or >20 lesions outside primary/adjacent dermatomes suggests dissemination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced VZV-specific cellular immunity permits virus to travel from sensory ganglion to skin
Neuronal inflammation/injury explains acute pain and persistent neuropathic symptoms

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical eruption → **clinical diagnosis**; atypical lesions → vesicle-base VZV PCR
Assess ocular, neurologic, and systemic findings; consider immunodeficiency evaluation for unusually severe/recurrent disease
CSF PCR for suspected CNS infection; do not delay treatment in high-risk presentations

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Valacyclovir, famciclovir, or acyclovir** ideally within 72 hours; still treat new lesions or complications
Dissemination, visceral/CNS disease, severe immunosuppression → **IV acyclovir**
Acute pain: acetaminophen/NSAID, add neuropathic agent when needed; avoid routine systemic steroids
Ramsay Hunt: antiviral plus glucocorticoid early; eye lubrication/protection for incomplete closure
Postherpetic neuralgia: gabapentin/pregabalin, topical lidocaine, selected TCA; no antiviral benefit after resolved eruption

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent pain >90 days, secondary bacterial infection, corneal injury, vision loss
Meningoencephalitis, vasculopathy, visceral spread in vulnerable patients

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Shingrix two doses** for adults ≥50 years or immunocompromised ≥19 years, including prior zoster
Cover lesions until crusted; exposure causes chickenpox in susceptible contacts, not immediate shingles
Disseminated: airborne/contact until crusted; immunocompromised localized: same precautions until dissemination excluded

rows.label: Mimics
items: HSV: recurrent localized lesions, often oral/genital rather than a full dermatome
Contact dermatitis: prominent itch, exposure pattern, no neuropathic prodrome

hiv-infection.name: HIV infection
hiv-infection.scope: Acute HIV, testing, ART start, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, PrEP/PEP, opportunistic infections (CMV retinitis, toxoplasmosis, PJP)
hiv-infection.core: HIV progressively depletes CD4 cells; early diagnosis and suppressive ART prevent immune failure and sexual transmission.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual exposure, shared injection equipment, perinatal transmission; other STIs increase acquisition risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Acute infection: fever, rash, sore throat, generalized lymphadenopathy after recent exposure
Weight loss, oral thrush, recurrent infections suggest advanced immunodeficiency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retroviral integration creates lifelong reservoirs; ongoing replication drives immune depletion and inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Fourth-generation Ag/Ab → HIV-1/2 differentiation assay**; discordance → HIV RNA
★ Recent exposure/acute syndrome despite negative screen → **HIV RNA**, before antibodies appear
Baseline viral load, CD4, resistance genotype, renal/liver function, HBV/HCV/TB testing; pregnancy assessment
AIDS: CD4 <200 or AIDS-defining illness regardless of count

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Start **integrase-based ART promptly**, usually bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine; assess HBV coinfection and interactions
Do not delay routine ART for genotype; cryptococcal/TB meningitis require disease-specific deferred timing
PJP: TMP-SMX; add glucocorticoid if PaO₂ <70 or A–a gradient ≥35
Toxoplasmosis: pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin or TMP-SMX; CMV retinitis: valganciclovir, urgent ophthalmology

rows.label: Complications
items: Opportunistic infections, malignancies, wasting, neurocognitive disease, kidney disease
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after ART; drug toxicity/interactions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ PJP prophylaxis: **TMP-SMX** with CD4 <200 before/starting ART; on ART, <100 or 100–200 with viremia
Toxoplasma IgG positive + CD4 <100 → prophylaxis; MAC <50 only without immediate effective ART
★ Exposure ≤72 hours → **28-day PEP: dolutegravir + TDF/emtricitabine**; do not delay for laboratory results
PrEP: TDF/emtricitabine, cabotegravir, or lenacapavir; exclude HIV first, continue serial testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: EBV mononucleosis: atypical lymphocytes, heterophile positivity; acute HIV can be heterophile-negative
Primary CNS lymphoma: often solitary brain lesion, fails empiric anti-Toxoplasma treatment

table.title: Advanced-disease syndromes
rows: Dry cough, hypoxemia, ground-glass; induced sputum/BAL

hypertensive-crises.name: Hypertensive crises
hypertensive-crises.scope: Hypertensive urgency, hypertensive emergency, hypertensive encephalopathy, aortic dissection, acute pulmonary edema, IV labetalol, nicardipine, nitroprusside
hypertensive-crises.core: Severe BP elevation becomes an emergency when new target-organ injury accompanies it; the number alone does not determine urgency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Missed antihypertensives, CKD, sympathomimetics; clonidine withdrawal
Pregnancy, renovascular disease, catecholamine excess

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Usually **>180/120 mm Hg** with AKI, ACS, pulmonary edema, stroke, or dissection
Encephalopathy: headache, confusion, seizures, visual disturbance; papilledema or retinal hemorrhages

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Autoregulatory failure → endothelial injury, microangiopathy, tissue ischemia; cerebral vasogenic edema in PRES

rows.label: Dx
items: Repeat correctly sized cuff reading; examine neurologic status, fundi, pulses, heart and lungs
Creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis, ECG; troponin with cardiac symptoms
Neurologic symptoms → head CT; suspected dissection → CTA chest/aorta
MRI posterior vasogenic edema supports PRES after hemorrhage exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Most emergencies: ICU, titratable IV **nicardipine or labetalol**
★ Reduce MAP ≤25% first hour → approximately 160/100–110 over 2–6 hours; then gradual normalization
★ No acute injury: treat pain/anxiety, restart or adjust oral drugs, arrange close outpatient follow-up
Avoid rapid IV lowering for asymptomatic BP; avoid immediate-release nifedipine
Nitroprusside: cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity with prolonged use or renal/hepatic dysfunction; monitor closely

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral hemorrhage, renal failure, MI; overly rapid lowering → cerebral/coronary hypoperfusion

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication access and adherence; home BP monitoring; avoid cocaine and amphetamines

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pain/anxiety elevation: improves after trigger control, no acute injury
Ischemic stroke: permissive hypertension thresholds differ; avoid applying generic reduction targets

increased-intracranial-pressure.name: Increased intracranial pressure
increased-intracranial-pressure.scope: Cushing triad, papilledema, ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, herniation syndromes, hyperosmolar therapy
increased-intracranial-pressure.core: Progressive headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness from raised intracranial pressure requires rapid distinction between mass effect, hydrocephalus, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, intracranial bleeding, tumor, cerebral edema, CNS infection, obstructed CSF flow
VP shunt: blockage or infection; IIH: obesity, reproductive-age women, tetracyclines, retinoids

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning/Valsalva headache, papilledema, diplopia from sixth-nerve palsy; infants may have bulging fontanelle
★ **Cushing triad**: hypertension/widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations; late dangerous finding
Uncal herniation → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral weakness; tonsillar herniation → respiratory arrest
IIH: pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations; shunt failure: recurrent headache, vomiting, lethargy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed skull volume: excess tissue, blood, or CSF raises pressure after compensatory reserve exhausted
Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP − ICP; falling perfusion worsens ischemia and edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable/acute deficit → **noncontrast head CT**; papilledema with stable suspected IIH → MRI + MRV
★ **No LP before excluding mass effect/obstructive hydrocephalus** when concerning signs present
IIH: normal imaging aside from supportive findings, normal CSF composition, opening pressure ≥25 cm H₂O
Shunt failure → head imaging, shunt series, urgent neurosurgery; normal ventricular size does not exclude obstruction

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Herniation concern → **airway support, head elevation, IV hypertonic saline or mannitol**, urgent neurosurgery
Avoid hypoxia/hypotension; brief controlled hyperventilation only as bridge for impending herniation
Hydrocephalus → CSF drainage/shunt revision; mass lesion → definitive decompression
Dexamethasone for tumor-associated vasogenic edema; no corticosteroids for traumatic brain injury
IIH → weight loss + acetazolamide; threatened vision → optic nerve fenestration or CSF diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent visual loss, ischemic injury, herniation, death
Hyperosmolar agents → electrolyte/renal disturbances; CSF devices → infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid causative drugs in IIH; follow visual fields and optic discs
Shunt education: prompt evaluation for recurrence or fever; injury prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Migraine: normal fundus and no progressive focal/mental-status findings
Cerebral venous thrombosis: venous obstruction on MRV, not idiopathic disease

increased-intracranial-pressure.evidence: Not checked online; established neurocritical care and IIH diagnostic principles.

inflammatory-myopathies.name: Inflammatory myopathies
inflammatory-myopathies.scope: Polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis, elevated creatine kinase, autoantibodies (anti-Jo-1, anti-Mi-2), muscle biopsy, malignancy screening, systemic corticosteroids
inflammatory-myopathies.core: Objective muscle weakness with elevated muscle enzymes suggests myopathy; distribution, skin findings, and biopsy distinguish treatable inflammation from inclusion body disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune predisposition; adult dermatomyositis associated with occult malignancy
Inclusion body myositis: usually men >50 years; review statin and other myotoxic exposures

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Difficulty rising or lifting arms**, neck flexor weakness; sensation generally preserved
Dysphagia, aspiration, dyspnea warrant evaluation for bulbar/respiratory weakness and interstitial lung disease
Dermatomyositis can have characteristic rash before significant muscle weakness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Polymyositis: T-cell-mediated endomysial injury; dermatomyositis: complement-associated microvascular injury
Inclusion body disease combines inflammatory and degenerative pathology, explaining poor immunosuppressive response

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK, aldolase, AST/ALT**, TSH; muscle can explain transaminase elevation without primary liver disease
MRI identifies edema and guides **muscle biopsy**; EMG supports a myopathic pattern
★ **Anti-Jo-1**: antisynthetase syndrome with ILD, arthritis, mechanic's hands; **anti-Mi-2**: classic dermatomyositis
Check swallowing and lung function when symptomatic; exclude inherited, endocrine, and drug-induced myopathies

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Polymyositis/dermatomyositis → **systemic glucocorticoids + steroid-sparing agent**, such as methotrexate or azathioprine
Severe/refractory disease or dysphagia → IVIG or other specialist-directed immunomodulation
Inclusion body: PT/OT, mobility aids, swallowing support; immunosuppression usually ineffective
Dermatomyositis rash: sun protection and topical agents; rehabilitation without prolonged immobilization

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, respiratory failure, ILD, myocarditis; juvenile dermatomyositis can cause calcinosis
Steroid myopathy causes new weakness with normal CK; treatment also increases infection and fracture risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adult dermatomyositis → **age-based plus risk-based malignancy evaluation**, especially near diagnosis
Bone protection, immunizations, infection prophylaxis according to immunosuppressive intensity; monitor strength and CK

rows.label: Mimics
items: Polymyalgia rheumatica: pain/stiffness without true weakness or ↑CK
Myasthenia: fatigability, ocular symptoms, normal CK; ALS: mixed UMN/LMN signs

table.title: Distribution and biopsy
rows: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl erythema

intracranial-hemorrhage.name: Intracranial hemorrhage
intracranial-hemorrhage.scope: Intracerebral hemorrhage, hypertensive hemorrhage, amyloid angiopathy, coagulopathy reversal, blood pressure management
intracranial-hemorrhage.core: Acute focal neurologic deficits with headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness require immediate CT to identify intraparenchymal bleeding and guide reversal.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Chronic hypertension, older age, anticoagulants/coagulopathy, stimulant use
Vascular malformation, tumor, venous thrombosis; lobar recurrence in older adults suggests cerebral amyloid angiopathy

rows.label: Clues
items: Rapid progression, seizure, severe BP elevation; small bleeds may resemble ischemic stroke
★ Hypertensive sites: **putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum**; amyloid favors superficial lobar locations
Declining consciousness, asymmetric pupils, abnormal posturing → mass effect/herniation
Cerebellar injury: vomiting, severe ataxia, vertigo; rapid deterioration possible despite initially preserved alertness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Small-artery lipohyalinosis or amyloid deposition weakens vessel walls
Expanding hematoma, intraventricular extension, and perihematomal edema cause secondary injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Noncontrast head CT now**; CBC/platelets, INR/PTT, renal function, glucose, medication history
CTA/vascular imaging for younger patients, atypical location, suspected malformation; repeat CT for deterioration/expansion
MRI susceptibility imaging identifies microbleeds and underlying lesions after stabilization
Do not give thrombolysis or perform LP for established parenchymal hemorrhage

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway, head elevation, neuro-ICU; **stop anticoagulants and reverse immediately**
★ Mild/moderate ICH, SBP 150–220 → IV **nicardipine/clevidipine**, target ~140, maintain 130–150 mm Hg
Large/severe ICH requires individualized perfusion goals; avoid abrupt excessive BP reduction or SBP <130
Cerebellar deterioration, hydrocephalus, brainstem compression, or volume ≥15 mL → **urgent surgical evacuation**
Hydrocephalus → ventricular drain; herniation → hypertonic saline/mannitol; treat seizures, no routine prophylaxis

rows.label: Complications
items: Hematoma expansion, hydrocephalus, herniation, seizures, disability, recurrent hemorrhage
★ **No routine platelet transfusion** for antiplatelet-associated ICH without emergency surgery/severe thrombocytopenia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Long-term BP control, smoking/stimulant cessation; reassess anticoagulation using recurrence and embolic risks
Intermittent pneumatic compression immediately; low-dose heparin prophylaxis after bleeding stability is documented

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ischemic stroke: no acute blood on CT; SAH: thunderclap, sulcal/cisternal blood
Hemorrhagic tumor: mass/edema pattern, enhancement; confirm with MRI

ischemic-stroke-and-tia.name: Ischemic stroke and TIA
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.scope: TIA (including amaurosis fugax), ischemic stroke, acute management (tPA, thrombectomy), secondary prevention, risk factors
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.core: Abrupt focal neurologic loss from cerebral ischemia; transient monocular blindness localizes to the ipsilateral carotid circulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hypertension, smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia, carotid atherosclerosis
Atrial fibrillation, recent MI, endocarditis, arterial dissection

rows.label: Clues
items: Aphasia or neglect suggests cortical involvement; crossed cranial-nerve/limb findings suggest brainstem disease
★ **Last known well** establishes treatment timing; symptom discovery time may differ
TIA: resolved deficit without acute infarction; urgent evaluation despite normal examination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Thromboembolism or small-vessel occlusion → infarct core surrounded by salvageable penumbra
Reperfusion preserves threatened tissue but increases hemorrhagic transformation risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Fingerstick glucose + **noncontrast head CT** first; normal early CT does not exclude ischemia
CTA head/neck for large-vessel occlusion; MRI diffusion for small infarcts or diagnostic uncertainty
ECG, telemetry, carotid imaging; echocardiography for suspected cardiac emboli

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling deficit, eligible ≤4.5 hours → **alteplase or tenecteplase**; imaging-selected extended windows possible
Thrombolysis: BP <185/110 before, <180/105 after; exclude bleeding and significant anticoagulant effect
★ Large-vessel occlusion → **mechanical thrombectomy**, selected cases through 24 hours; do not delay thrombolysis
No reperfusion: generally allow BP ≤220/120; oxygen for hypoxemia; swallow assessment before oral intake
Aspirin after hemorrhage excluded; after thrombolysis, wait 24 hours and repeat imaging

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral edema, aspiration, venous thrombosis, seizures, disability

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Minor noncardioembolic stroke/high-risk TIA → short **aspirin + clopidogrel**, then single antiplatelet
AF → oral anticoagulation with timing based on infarct/bleeding risk; high-intensity statin, BP control
Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70–99% → endarterectomy when eligible; selected 50–69% also benefit

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypoglycemia: deficit reverses with glucose
Migraine aura: spreading positive symptoms; seizure: witnessed convulsion followed by Todd paralysis

lead-poisoning.name: Lead poisoning
lead-poisoning.scope: Occupational exposure, moonshine, pediatric lead toxicity, basophilic stippling, motor neuropathy (wrist drop, foot drop), encephalopathy, dimercaprol, succimer chelation
lead-poisoning.core: Exposure-related abdominal colic, anemia, and neurologic dysfunction; children may have developmental injury despite appearing well.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pre-1978 paint dust, contaminated water/soil, imported remedies or pottery; pica increases exposure
Battery manufacture/recycling, construction, firing ranges, moonshine; occupational dust carried home

rows.label: Clues
items: Children: irritability, constipation, learning/behavior problems; severe cases → seizures, encephalopathy
Adults: **motor-predominant neuropathy** with wrist/foot drop, hypertension, renal dysfunction
Microcytic or normocytic anemia; basophilic stippling supportive but neither sensitive nor specific

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inhibition of ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase → impaired heme synthesis
Calcium mimicry disrupts neuronal signaling; deposition in bone creates long-lived stores

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Venous blood lead level** confirms elevated capillary screening; do not rely on hair testing
★ Pediatric reference **3.5 µg/dL** triggers exposure intervention; no safe childhood level
CBC, iron studies, renal function; abdominal radiograph for suspected ingested lead objects/paint chips
Developmental assessment; assess siblings and household exposure

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove exposure; involve environmental health/toxicology; correct iron deficiency and support calcium intake
Child **45–69 µg/dL**, no encephalopathy → oral succimer with expert supervision
★ Encephalopathy or ≥70 µg/dL → admit; **dimercaprol followed by calcium disodium EDTA**
