Radiopaque lead in bowel → polyethylene glycol whole-bowel irrigation when safe
Adults: chelation depends on symptoms and level; never apply pediatric thresholds automatically

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent cognitive deficits despite chelation; CKD, infertility, pregnancy complications
EDTA can injure kidneys; disodium EDTA causes fatal hypocalcemia—use calcium disodium formulation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Certified lead abatement, wet cleaning, occupational protective measures; avoid contaminated products
Medicaid childhood screening at 12 and 24 months; otherwise risk/local screening program

rows.label: Mimics
items: Iron deficiency: low ferritin; can coexist and increase lead absorption
AIP: marked urinary PBG elevation, no characteristic lead anemia

low-back-pain.name: Low back pain
low-back-pain.scope: Lumbosacral strain, herniated disk and radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, red flags, imaging indications, conservative management
low-back-pain.core: Most acute low back pain improves with activity and analgesia; neurologic deficits or systemic red flags change the workup.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heavy lifting, deconditioning, obesity, prolonged sitting
Cancer, immunosuppression, injection drug use, osteoporosis, chronic glucocorticoids increase serious-pathology risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Mechanical pain varies with movement; isolated axial pain without systemic illness favors benign disease
★ **Urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bilateral weakness** → cauda equina emergency
Fever, weight loss, night pain, trauma, or progressive weakness → targeted urgent evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Paraspinal injury causes localized pain; degenerative narrowing or disk extrusion compresses neural structures

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ No red flags → **no initial imaging**, including routine radiographs
Focused strength, reflex, sensory, gait examination; straight-leg raise supports lower lumbar radiculopathy
★ Suspected infection, malignancy, cord compression → **MRI**; suspected fracture → radiograph or CT
Persistent symptoms despite about 6 weeks' care → MRI if intervention being considered
Suspected spinal infection → ESR/CRP, blood cultures; normal temperature does not exclude infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Continue activity**, superficial heat, short NSAID course; avoid prolonged bed rest
Physical rehabilitation for persistent symptoms; avoid routine opioids and systemic steroids
Progressive motor deficit or cauda equina → urgent surgical decompression
Refractory disabling radicular pain → epidural injection or diskectomy after imaging correlation

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic pain, functional limitation, medication dependence
Untreated compression → permanent bladder, bowel, sexual, or motor dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Core strengthening, regular exercise, ergonomic lifting, weight management
Return to usual tasks gradually; address fear avoidance and workplace barriers

rows.label: Mimics
items: AAA: abdominal pulsatile mass, vascular risk, hypotension
Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; inflammatory back pain: improves with exercise

table.title: Mechanical patterns
rows: Leg pain below knee; cough aggravates

low-back-pain.evidence: Not checked online; established generalist back-pain evaluation.

lyme-disease.name: Lyme disease
lyme-disease.scope: Borrelia burgdorferi, erythema migrans, early localized, early disseminated, late Lyme arthritis, doxycycline, ceftriaxone
lyme-disease.core: Ixodes-transmitted Borrelia infection progresses from an expanding skin lesion to neurologic, cardiac, or joint disease when untreated.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Wooded/brush exposure in Northeast, mid-Atlantic, upper Midwest; attached blacklegged tick
Tick exposure may be unnoticed; small-mammal reservoirs sustain transmission

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Erythema migrans**: enlarging lesion >5 cm, days after bite; central clearing not required
Early dissemination: multiple lesions, facial palsy, lymphocytic meningitis, fluctuating AV block
Late disease: intermittent large-joint swelling, especially knee; severe pain less prominent than effusion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Spirochete inoculation → local multiplication, hematogenous spread, inflammatory injury
Persistent antibodies can remain after cure and do not prove viable infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical erythema migrans → **clinical diagnosis**, no serology needed
Other compatible disease → two-tier serology: EIA followed by immunoblot or second EIA
Early localized serology may be negative; isolated IgM after >30 days is unreliable
Joint-fluid PCR supports selected arthritis cases; CSF testing for CNS disease; ECG for cardiac symptoms

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Localized skin disease → **doxycycline 10 days**, or amoxicillin/cefuroxime 14 days
Facial palsy/mild neurologic disease may use oral doxycycline; severe CNS disease → IV ceftriaxone
★ Symptomatic carditis, PR ≥300 ms, higher-degree block → **hospitalize, telemetry, IV ceftriaxone**; pacing if needed
Lyme arthritis → 28-day oral course; persistent objective disease requires reassessment, sometimes IV ceftriaxone
Post-treatment nonspecific fatigue → supportive evaluation; no prolonged antibiotics without objective reinfection/failure

rows.label: Complications
items: Complete heart block, meningoencephalitis, recurrent arthritis, postinfectious joint inflammation
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction shortly after antibiotics; not necessarily drug allergy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ High-risk Ixodes bite, attachment ≥36 hours, endemic region → **single-dose doxycycline within 72 hours of removal**
Tick checks, permethrin-treated clothing, DEET; remove tick with fine tweezers near skin
No prophylaxis for low-risk bite or routine serologic testing of asymptomatic patients

rows.label: Mimics
items: Immediate bite hypersensitivity: small, itchy, does not progressively enlarge
Septic arthritis: marked pain, toxicity, positive culture; babesiosis: hemolysis and intraerythrocytic parasites

multiple-sclerosis.name: Multiple sclerosis
multiple-sclerosis.scope: Relapsing-remitting, optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion), Uhthoff phenomenon, Lhermitte sign, disease-modifying therapies
multiple-sclerosis.core: Neurologic deficits separated in location and time, often including optic neuritis, suggest inflammatory CNS demyelination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young adulthood, female sex, family history; EBV exposure, smoking and low vitamin D association

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Optic neuritis: **pain with eye movement**, monocular visual loss, impaired color vision, afferent pupillary defect
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: **MLF lesion**, impaired adduction with contralateral abducting nystagmus
Uhthoff: old deficits worsen with heat; Lhermitte: neck flexion triggers electric spinal sensation
Transverse myelitis: weakness, sensory level, urinary dysfunction; acute relapse generally lasts >24 hours

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated oligodendrocyte/myelin injury → CNS plaques, conduction block and eventual axonal loss
Relapsing-remitting: attacks with recovery; progressive forms: accumulating disability between or without attacks

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **MRI brain/cord**: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal lesions; 2024 criteria add optic nerve
Classic time dissemination: new follow-up lesion or simultaneous enhancing/nonenhancing lesions; exclude better explanation
CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands support diagnosis; revised criteria also accept kappa free-light-chain index
Atypical severe visual loss/long cord lesion → serum AQP4/MOG antibodies; revised criteria permit selected earlier diagnoses
Suspected relapse → exclude fever, UTI and metabolic triggers before escalating immunosuppression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling relapse → **high-dose methylprednisolone**; severe steroid-refractory attack → plasma exchange
★ Relapsing disease → early disease-modifying drug, e.g., **ocrelizumab**, tailored to activity and pregnancy plans
Lower-activity options include interferon-beta or glatiramer; natalizumab requires JC-virus/PML risk assessment
Baclofen for spasticity; rehabilitation, bladder care and treatment of neuropathic pain
Isolated heat/infection-related worsening → treat trigger; not automatically a new inflammatory attack

rows.label: Complications
items: Gait impairment, falls, neurogenic bladder, depression and cognitive dysfunction
Immunosuppressive treatment → infection; some agents carry PML risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, vaccination; review contraception/pregnancy before disease-modifying drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: symmetric posterior-column dysfunction, macrocytosis
NMOSD: AQP4-positive, often severe attacks; some MS drugs worsen disease
Stroke: abrupt maximal deficit, vascular territory

neonatal-sepsis.name: Neonatal sepsis
neonatal-sepsis.scope: Early-onset neonatal sepsis, late-onset neonatal sepsis, Group B Streptococcus, Listeria, ampicillin and gentamicin
neonatal-sepsis.core: A newborn with temperature instability, feeding difficulty, apnea, or unexplained deterioration may have invasive infection despite subtle examination findings.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Prematurity, maternal GBS, membrane rupture ≥18 hours**, intra-amniotic infection
Late disease: central lines, ventilation, prolonged hospitalization, disrupted skin/GI barriers

rows.label: Clues
items: Hypothermia or fever, lethargy, irritability, poor suck, jaundice, vomiting or glucose instability
Respiratory distress, desaturation, mottling, delayed capillary refill; hypotension is a late sign
Bulging fontanelle or seizures suggest meningitis; vesicles, hepatitis or maternal HSV suggest herpes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immature innate/adaptive immunity permits rapid hematogenous spread
Maternal genital organisms seed early disease; later acquisition includes community and healthcare organisms

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Ill neonate → **blood culture before antibiotics**, CBC and inflammatory markers as adjuncts
LP when safe for suspected meningitis, positive blood culture, critical illness or poor response
Urine culture useful in late-onset evaluation; not routinely needed for immediate early-onset disease
Never delay antibiotics for LP in instability; normal WBC/CRP does not exclude infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early-onset empiric treatment → **ampicillin + gentamicin** after cultures
Suspected meningitis → ampicillin plus cefotaxime where available, tailored to local resistance and cultures
NICU late-onset disease → antistaphylococcal plus gram-negative coverage; vancomycin when MRSA/line resistance risk
★ HSV concern → **IV acyclovir** plus HSV testing; avoid ceftriaxone in neonates
Respiratory/perfusion support; if cultures negative and infant well, stop empiric antibiotics at 36–48 hours

rows.label: Complications
items: Septic shock, DIC, meningitis, hearing loss, neurodevelopmental injury or death
Gentamicin → renal/ototoxicity; unnecessary antibiotics alter microbiome and increase resistant infection risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Maternal **GBS screening and intrapartum penicillin** for positive/eligible high-risk mothers
Hand/line hygiene; well exposed infants ≥35 weeks → serial exams or sepsis-risk calculator strategy

rows.label: Mimics
items: RDS/TTN: delivery-related respiratory pattern without systemic infection evidence
Hypoglycemia or duct-dependent cardiac disease: metabolic/cardiac testing identifies cause

table.title: Common organisms
rows: GBS, E coli; less often Listeria
Coagulase-negative staphylococci, S aureus, gram-negatives, Candida
GBS, E coli, other enteric bacteria

neuromuscular-junction-disorders.name: Neuromuscular junction disorders
neuromuscular-junction-disorders.scope: Myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, botulism, repetitive nerve stimulation, autoantibodies
neuromuscular-junction-disorders.core: Fluctuating or descending weakness with preserved sensation localizes to neuromuscular transmission; reflexes, pupils, and exercise response separate major causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: MG: autoimmune disease, thymoma; LEMS: smoking/small-cell lung carcinoma
Botulism: improperly canned foods, injection wounds, infant honey or environmental spores

rows.label: Clues
items: MG: diplopia, ptosis, nasal speech, chewing fatigue; worse late day or repeated activity
LEMS: proximal leg weakness, dry mouth, constipation; transient strength/reflex improvement after exertion
Botulism: cranial palsies → symmetric descending paralysis, autonomic dysfunction; infant constipation and floppy weakness
★ **Bulbar weakness or declining ventilation** → impending respiratory failure even with normal oxygen saturation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: MG: postsynaptic receptor/MuSK autoimmunity; LEMS: presynaptic voltage-gated calcium-channel autoimmunity
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins → impaired acetylcholine release

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **AChR antibodies**, then MuSK if negative; repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fiber EMG
MG → chest CT for thymoma; bedside ice-pack improvement supports ocular disease
LEMS → P/Q calcium-channel antibodies and chest CT for cancer
★ Suspected crisis → serial **forced vital capacity/negative inspiratory force**; not pulse oximetry alone
Botulism → serum/stool/toxin testing via public health; treatment before confirmation

rows.label: Tx
items: MG → pyridostigmine, steroid-sparing immunosuppression; thymectomy for thymoma or selected generalized AChR-positive disease
★ Myasthenic crisis → **airway support + IVIG or plasma exchange**, treat precipitant
LEMS → amifampridine and treatment of malignancy; immunotherapy for persistent autoimmune disease
★ Botulism → **heptavalent antitoxin**; infants → human botulism immune globulin; ventilatory support
Wound botulism → debridement/antibiotics; avoid aminoglycosides and magnesium with impaired junctional transmission

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, respiratory arrest; MG immunosuppression → infection; steroids may initially worsen weakness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Review MG-exacerbating drugs; safe food preservation; no honey before age 1 year
LEMS → ongoing cancer surveillance if initial evaluation negative

rows.label: Mimics
items: Guillain-Barré: usually ascending weakness and areflexia, possible sensory symptoms
Brainstem stroke: abrupt focal signs; motor neuron disease: fasciculations/UMN signs

neuromuscular-junction-disorders.evidence: Botulism checked 2026-10-30: [CDC clinical guidelines](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/rr/rr7002a1.htm); MG/LEMS: established teaching.

normal-pressure-hydrocephalus.name: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
normal-pressure-hydrocephalus.scope: Triad (gait apraxia/magnetic gait, cognitive impairment, urinary urgency/incontinence), ventriculomegaly on neuroimaging, high-volume lumbar puncture (Miller Fisher test), ventriculoperitoneal shunt
normal-pressure-hydrocephalus.core: An older adult develops a magnetic, short-stepped gait followed by slowed thinking and urinary urgency, with enlarged ventricles.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Often idiopathic in older adults; secondary to subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, head trauma

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Gait impairment first and most prominent**: initiation difficulty, broad base, unstable turns
Frontal-subcortical dysfunction: apathy, slowed processing, executive impairment rather than early isolated amnesia
Urinary urgency can precede incontinence; complete triad unnecessary
Prominent focal deficits, severe early memory loss, or resting tremor suggest another diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impaired CSF absorption → ventricular expansion and dysfunction of periventricular frontal-subcortical pathways
Lumbar opening pressure often normal despite disordered CSF dynamics

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Brain MRI or CT**: ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal atrophy; Evans index >0.3 supportive
MRI may show tight high-convexity sulci, enlarged Sylvian fissures and periventricular signal change
★ **High-volume LP, 30–50 mL**; compare standardized gait testing before and after drainage
Improvement supports shunt responsiveness; negative tap does not exclude—consider extended lumbar drainage
Exclude obstructive hydrocephalus and assess competing neurodegenerative/vascular disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Selected symptomatic candidates → **ventriculoperitoneal shunt**; gait most likely to improve
Rehabilitation, fall precautions, bladder support; counsel that advanced dementia improves less reliably
No established medication reverses idiopathic NPH

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated: falls, dependence; shunt infection, obstruction, overdrainage-related subdural hematoma
Recurrent symptoms after initial benefit → evaluate shunt malfunction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alzheimer disease: early episodic memory loss, proportional cortical atrophy
Parkinson disease: asymmetric bradykinesia/rigidity, resting tremor, levodopa response
Hydrocephalus ex vacuo: ventricles and sulci enlarge together from tissue loss

normal-pressure-hydrocephalus.evidence: Not checked online; established NPH evaluation and shunt-selection teaching.

osteonecrosis.name: Osteonecrosis
osteonecrosis.scope: Avascular necrosis of femoral head, risk factors (corticosteroids, alcohol, sickle cell, trauma), MRI sensitivity, crescent sign on plain radiograph, core decompression, joint replacement
osteonecrosis.core: Progressive deep hip or groin pain after steroid exposure, heavy alcohol use, sickle cell disease, or trauma suggests femoral-head ischemia.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Glucocorticoids**, excessive alcohol, sickle cell vaso-occlusion, femoral neck fracture or hip dislocation
SLE, transplantation, decompression exposure; bilateral disease common with systemic causes

rows.label: Clues
items: Weight-bearing pain progressing to rest/night pain; limited internal rotation and abduction
Antalgic gait, referred thigh/knee pain; early examination can be nearly normal
Sudden worsening suggests subchondral fracture or articular collapse

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Interrupted subchondral blood supply → osteocyte death, microfractures, eventual joint surface collapse
Repair cannot keep pace with mechanical loading; secondary degenerative arthritis follows

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **AP pelvis and lateral hip radiographs** first; early disease may be radiographically occult
★ Persistent suspicion despite normal films → **MRI**, most sensitive early test
Later films: patchy sclerosis/lucency; crescent sign indicates subchondral fracture, then flattening
Evaluate contralateral hip when symptoms or systemic risk suggest bilateral involvement

rows.label: Tx
items: Protected weight-bearing, cane/crutches, NSAIDs, orthopedic referral; analgesics do not restore perfusion
★ Before collapse → **core decompression** in selected symptomatic lesions; joint-preserving options depend on extent
Advanced collapse or secondary arthritis → total hip arthroplasty
Reduce avoidable steroid/alcohol exposure; manage sickle cell and other underlying disorders

rows.label: Complications
items: Femoral-head collapse, painful osteoarthritis, loss of mobility and function
Arthroplasty: infection, dislocation, loosening; younger patients may require revision

rows.label: Prevention
items: Use lowest effective glucocorticoid exposure; counsel against heavy alcohol consumption
Prompt reduction of traumatic hip dislocation limits ischemic time; monitor high-risk post-traumatic hips
Activity modification during evaluation reduces loading on vulnerable subchondral bone

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hip osteoarthritis: gradual activity pain, joint-space narrowing and osteophytes rather than early isolated necrosis
Septic arthritis: fever, severe pain with passive motion; urgent aspiration
Femoral neck stress fracture: overuse, fracture line or marrow edema on MRI

osteonecrosis.evidence: Not checked online; established orthopedic diagnosis and stage-based treatment.

parkinson-disease.name: Parkinson disease
parkinson-disease.scope: Cardinal motor symptoms (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability/pull test), nonmotor symptoms, dopamine agonists, levodopa-carbidopa, atypical parkinsonism (PSP, MSA)
parkinson-disease.core: Progressive asymmetric bradykinesia with characteristic motor signs and levodopa responsiveness suggests Parkinson disease; early atypical features prompt another diagnosis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, family susceptibility, some pesticide exposures; most disease sporadic
Dopamine-blocking antipsychotics/metoclopramide cause secondary parkinsonism rather than idiopathic disease

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Resting pill-rolling tremor, cogwheel rigidity**, reduced arm swing, shuffling gait
Freezing, micrographia, hypophonia; pull test reveals impaired postural recovery, typically later
Constipation, anosmia, REM sleep behavior disorder, depression and autonomic symptoms can precede motor disease
Early severe falls, gaze palsy, marked autonomic failure or poor treatment response → atypical syndrome

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Substantia nigra dopaminergic neuron loss; α-synuclein Lewy bodies
Reduced striatal dopamine disrupts basal ganglia motor regulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; bradykinesia plus resting tremor and/or rigidity
Brain MRI for atypical findings; dopamine transporter imaging if uncertain degenerative versus nondegenerative tremor
Review medications; assess cognition, orthostatic BP, gait and swallowing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Function-limiting motor symptoms → **carbidopa/levodopa**, preferred initial dopaminergic treatment
Pramipexole/ropinirole for selected younger patients; avoid with hallucinations, impulse-control problems or age >70
Wearing-off → adjust levodopa schedule, add MAO-B/COMT inhibitor; dyskinesia → amantadine
★ Exercise, physical/speech/swallow rehabilitation; selected refractory fluctuations/tremor → **deep brain stimulation**
Psychosis → reduce provoking drugs; pimavanserin or selected quetiapine/clozapine, avoid potent dopamine blockers

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, dementia; medication → hallucinations, orthostasis, motor fluctuations/dyskinesias
Dopamine agonists → gambling/hypersexuality and sleep attacks; abrupt withdrawal → severe rigidity/hyperthermia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Fall-proof home, medication adherence, aspiration-risk assessment; no established primary neuroprotective treatment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Essential tremor: action/postural tremor without decrementing bradykinesia
Drug-induced: blocker exposure, often symmetric; normal-pressure hydrocephalus: magnetic gait, urinary/cognitive symptoms

table.title: Atypical parkinsonism
rows: Severe orthostasis/urinary dysfunction, possible cerebellar signs
Dementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism

physiologic-changes-of-aging.name: Physiologic changes of aging
physiologic-changes-of-aging.scope: Neurologic changes, sensory changes (presbyopia, presbycusis), sleep architecture changes (early wake, reduced total sleep), cardiovascular stiffening, renal decline, pulmonary compliance
physiologic-changes-of-aging.core: Normal aging reduces organ reserve; preserved everyday independence distinguishes expected slowing from disease.

rows.label: Definition
items: Gradual changes across systems; marked disability requires evaluation rather than attribution to age

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ Slower processing and recall; **orientation and learned knowledge preserved**
★ Less slow-wave sleep, more awakenings, earlier sleep/wake timing; modestly reduced total sleep
Presbyopia: reduced accommodation; presbycusis: bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss

rows.label: Use when
items: Reduced baroreflexes and maximal heart rate → orthostatic susceptibility, reduced exercise capacity
Lower renal clearance → adjust renally eliminated drugs despite normal-looking creatinine
Decreased vital capacity and cough reserve → greater respiratory illness vulnerability

rows.label: Compare
items: ★ **Arterial stiffness** → widened pulse pressure; ventricular relaxation slows
Reduced lung elastic recoil → increased lung compliance; chest wall compliance decreases
Declining concentration/dilution → fluid imbalance; reduced muscle mass lowers creatinine production

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Delirium, dementia, falls, incontinence** require evaluation; never inevitable normal aging
Depression or sedatives can explain daytime sleepiness; severe insomnia needs investigation
Unilateral hearing loss, focal weakness, or rapidly progressive memory loss → disease workup

physiologic-changes-of-aging.evidence: Not checked online; established geriatric physiology.

porphyrias.name: Porphyrias
porphyrias.scope: Acute intermittent porphyria (PBG deaminase, abdominal pain, neuropathy, psychiatric symptoms, drug triggers, hemin, glucose), porphyria cutanea tarda (UROD deficiency, photosensitivity, blisters, phlebotomy)
porphyrias.core: Neurovisceral attacks and fragile sun-exposed skin represent different heme-pathway disorders; identify the accumulated precursor before choosing treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: AIP: autosomal dominant, low penetrance; fasting, alcohol, progesterone, CYP-inducing drugs trigger attacks
PCT: iron overload, hepatitis C, alcohol, estrogen, HIV; usually acquired

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ AIP: severe **abdominal pain without peritonitis**, constipation, tachycardia, psychiatric changes
Motor neuropathy, darkening urine, SIADH-related hyponatremia; **no photosensitivity** in AIP
PCT: dorsal hand blisters, skin fragility, hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: AIP: porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency → neurotoxic ALA/PBG accumulation
PCT: uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency → photoreactive porphyrin accumulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Acute attack → random **urine PBG, ALA, creatinine**, ideally before hemin; protect from light
PCT: plasma/urine porphyrins; evaluate ferritin, transferrin saturation, HCV, HIV
Genetic testing confirms subtype after biochemical diagnosis; normal attack PBG argues against AIP

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe AIP → **IV hemin**; stop triggers, analgesia, monitor respiratory strength and sodium
Mild attacks: carbohydrate loading; glucose while awaiting hemin, never delay hemin for severe disease
PCT: serial **phlebotomy**; low-dose hydroxychloroquine alternative when phlebotomy unsuitable
Treat HCV and iron overload; recurrent AIP → specialist consideration of givosiran

rows.label: Complications
items: AIP: respiratory paralysis, seizures, CKD; hepatic cancer risk
PCT: chronic liver disease; excessive phlebotomy → iron-deficiency anemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Avoid **barbiturates, phenytoin, carbamazepine** in AIP; check porphyria drug-safety lists
Regular nutrition; PCT sun protection, alcohol cessation, discontinue estrogen when feasible

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lead toxicity: anemia/basophilic stippling, elevated ALA without marked PBG elevation
Pseudoporphyria: similar blisters, normal porphyrin testing; often naproxen or dialysis

retinal-vascular-occlusion.name: Retinal vascular occlusion
retinal-vascular-occlusion.scope: Central retinal artery occlusion (pale retina, cherry-red fovea, ocular massage), branch retinal artery occlusion, central retinal vein occlusion (blood and thunder, optic disc edema), branch retinal vein occlusion
retinal-vascular-occlusion.core: Sudden painless monocular visual loss requires urgent funduscopic localization and immediate assessment for retinal ischemia or venous obstruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Arterial: carotid atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, giant cell arteritis
Venous: hypertension, diabetes, glaucoma, hyperviscosity; atypical young cases warrant targeted systemic evaluation

rows.label: Clues
items: Severe asymmetric retinal ischemia → relative afferent pupillary defect
Transient monocular blackout may precede permanent arterial occlusion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Arterial inflow obstruction → inner retinal infarction; venous outflow obstruction → hemorrhage and edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Dilated fundus examination** urgently; OCT quantifies macular edema
★ Retinal artery occlusion → **stroke-center evaluation**, carotid imaging, ECG and cardiac source assessment
Age >50 with headache, jaw claudication or scalp tenderness → ESR/CRP, CBC for GCA
Fluorescein angiography assesses venous nonperfusion and neovascularization risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ CRAO → immediate emergency/stroke referral; selected early cases → **IV thrombolysis consideration**
Suspected arteritic occlusion → immediate high-dose corticosteroids; never wait for temporal artery biopsy
★ **Ocular massage/paracentesis**: historical answers; unproven, potentially harmful, not recommended by AHA
Venous occlusion with vision-limiting macular edema → intravitreal **anti-VEGF** such as aflibercept
Retinal/iris neovascularization → retinal laser; systemic anticoagulation not routine for isolated vein occlusion

rows.label: Complications
items: Arterial occlusion: permanent blindness and future ischemic stroke
Venous occlusion: recurrent macular edema, vitreous hemorrhage, neovascular glaucoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: Control BP, diabetes, lipids, smoking; arterial disease → antiplatelet/statin or anticoagulation according to embolic source
Ophthalmic surveillance after venous occlusion for delayed neovascularization

rows.label: Mimics
items: Retinal detachment: flashes, floaters, curtain-like field loss
Acute angle closure: painful red eye, halos, high IOP

table.title: Fundus pattern
rows: Sectoral retinal whitening; corresponding field defect

somatic-symptom-disorders.name: Somatic symptom disorders
somatic-symptom-disorders.scope: Somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, conversion disorder, factitious disorder, malingering, regular scheduled visits, validating suffering
somatic-symptom-disorders.core: Distressing symptoms or health fears require a positive psychiatric formulation, validation, and proportionate medical evaluation; intent separates factitious behavior from functional symptoms.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, anxiety/depression, chronic illness, major stress; medical and psychiatric disorders can coexist

rows.label: Clues
items: Persistent reassurance seeking, repeated testing, high health-related distress, impaired function
Assess suicidality, abuse, substance use, and medication-related symptoms; avoid assumptions based on demographics

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Attention, threat appraisal, and learned responses amplify suffering; symptoms do not require conscious production
External reward differs from internal sick-role motivation; neither can be inferred from one inconsistency

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Somatic symptom disorder does not require medically unexplained symptoms**; excessive response is decisive
Illness anxiety requires ≥6 months preoccupation; somatic symptom persistence typically >6 months
★ Functional neurologic disorder: **positive incompatible examination signs**, such as Hoover sign, support diagnosis
New objective abnormalities still warrant targeted medical evaluation; avoid diagnosing solely by exhaustive exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **One clinician, scheduled visits**, focused examinations; validate suffering without endorsing unproven disease
CBT, functional rehabilitation, treat comorbid anxiety/depression; explain functional neurologic mechanisms nonjudgmentally
★ Avoid repeated low-value procedures; **new red flags → reassess**, regardless of established psychiatric diagnosis
Factitious: coordinated team, factual records, supportive discussion; protect dependents from induced illness

rows.label: Complications
items: Iatrogenic injury, unnecessary surgery, opioid exposure, disability, fragmented care
Factitious disorder imposed on another → serious abuse risk requiring safeguarding action

rows.label: Mimics
items: Occult medical disease: evolving objective findings or coherent physiologic abnormalities
Delusional disorder: fixed somatic belief despite evidence, without flexible doubt

table.title: Distinguishing patterns
rows: Motor/sensory symptoms incompatible with neurologic disease
Intentional deception; no obvious external reward

somatic-symptom-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established DSM-5-TR teaching.

spinal-cord-compression.name: Spinal cord compression
spinal-cord-compression.scope: Neoplastic spinal cord compression (epidural metastases, dexamethasone, emergent MRI), spinal epidural abscess (fever, IV drug use, empiric antibiotics), cauda equina syndrome, surgical decompression
spinal-cord-compression.core: Back pain with new weakness, sensory changes or sphincter dysfunction requires urgent MRI to identify reversible neural compression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known breast, prostate, lung, renal cancer or myeloma → epidural metastases
IV drug use, bacteremia, diabetes, spinal procedure or immunosuppression → epidural abscess
Large lumbar disc herniation, trauma or spinal stenosis → cauda equina compression

rows.label: Clues
items: Progressive nocturnal pain, pain with cough/strain, radicular symptoms; deficits may be initially subtle
Cord lesion: sensory level, spastic weakness, hyperreflexia below lesion after acute phase
★ Cauda equina: **saddle anesthesia, urinary retention**, reduced anal tone, asymmetric flaccid leg weakness
Epidural abscess: fever/back pain ± deficit; classic triad often incomplete

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Epidural tumor, infection or disc material compresses neural tissue and impairs blood supply
Longstanding compression produces irreversible ischemic injury; bladder dysfunction signals advanced disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urgent contrast MRI** of suspected region; whole spine for suspected metastatic compression
Postvoid residual supports retention assessment but normal result does not exclude early cauda equina syndrome
Suspected abscess → blood cultures, CBC, ESR/CRP; image before LP
MRI unavailable/contraindicated → CT myelography; ordinary radiographs cannot exclude epidural pathology

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Malignant compression with deficit → **dexamethasone immediately**, urgent neurosurgery/radiation consultation
Tumor → decompression/stabilization ± radiotherapy; choice depends on stability, neurologic function and prognosis
★ Epidural abscess → **vancomycin + cefepime**, cultures; urgent decompression for deficits or instability
Cauda equina syndrome → emergency spinal surgical assessment and **decompression**
Immobilize if instability suspected; bladder drainage and analgesia during definitive treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent paralysis, bowel/bladder dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, pressure injuries and VTE
Abscess → sepsis; steroids can worsen uncontrolled infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Rapid assessment of cancer-associated new back pain; sterile procedures and prompt bacteremia treatment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mechanical strain: normal neurologic exam, no sphincter symptoms
Transverse myelitis: intrinsic cord lesion without external compression
Peripheral neuropathy: distal symmetric findings without sensory level

spinal-cord-compression.evidence: Not checked online; established neurologic and oncologic emergency principles.

subarachnoid-hemorrhage.name: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
subarachnoid-hemorrhage.scope: Ruptured saccular aneurysm, thunderclap headache, noncontrast head CT, lumbar puncture and xanthochromia, nimodipine, complications
subarachnoid-hemorrhage.core: Sudden headache maximal within seconds, often during exertion, with possible meningismus or collapse: presume subarachnoid hemorrhage until excluded.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, hypertension, family history, prior aneurysm; autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
Ruptured saccular aneurysm usually near circle-of-Willis branch points; cocaine increases rupture risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Vomiting, photophobia, neck stiffness, transient loss of consciousness; sentinel headache may precede major hemorrhage
★ **Painful pupil-involving CN III palsy** → posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Declining consciousness, focal deficits or seizures → high-risk presentation; normal examination does not exclude hemorrhage

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Blood enters subarachnoid space → meningeal irritation, ↑ICP, impaired CSF resorption
Blood-breakdown products and vascular injury contribute to delayed cerebral ischemia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Noncontrast head CT immediately**; sensitivity declines with elapsed time
★ Negative CT >6 hours after onset or neurologic deficit → **LP**, assessing xanthochromia and RBCs
High-quality CT within 6 hours, neurologically intact, expert interpretation → may exclude SAH without routine LP
Confirmed blood → **CT angiography**; negative/inconclusive CTA with suspected aneurysm → catheter angiography
Traumatic tap may show falling RBCs; clearing alone cannot reliably exclude SAH

rows.label: Tx
items: Support airway, reverse anticoagulation, analgesia; severe hypertension → IV nicardipine; avoid hypotension/BP swings
★ **Urgent aneurysm coiling or clipping**, preferably within 24 hours, prevents rebleeding
★ **Enteral nimodipine for 21 days**, maintain euvolemia; no prophylactic hypervolemia
Acute symptomatic hydrocephalus → external ventricular drainage
Secured aneurysm + delayed ischemia → induced hypertension; refractory → endovascular vasodilator/angioplasty

rows.label: Complications
items: Early rebleeding, hydrocephalus, seizures; delayed ischemia typically days 3–14
Hyponatremia from SIADH or cerebral salt wasting; stress cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, pulmonary edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation and BP control; specialist screening discussion for ≥2 affected first-degree relatives or high-risk ADPKD

rows.label: Mimics
items: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction: recurrent thunderclap headaches; segmental angiographic narrowing
Meningitis: fever and inflammatory CSF rather than aneurysmal bleeding
Migraine: usually slower onset, recurrent stereotyped episodes; first thunderclap still needs hemorrhage evaluation

syncope.name: Syncope
syncope.scope: Vasovagal / neurocardiogenic syncope, orthostatic syncope, situational syncope, cardiogenic syncope, breath-holding spells, cerebral hypoperfusion workup
syncope.core: Brief loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion with rapid spontaneous recovery; identify cardiac danger before labeling an episode reflex-mediated.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Dehydration, blood loss, autonomic dysfunction, diuretics/vasodilators; prolonged standing, heat, fear
Structural heart disease, conduction disease, arrhythmias, family history of sudden death

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Exertional or supine syncope**, palpitations, absent prodrome, cardiac murmur → high-risk cause
Reflex prodrome: nausea, warmth, diaphoresis, tunnel vision; may include brief myoclonic jerks
Situational triggers: urination, coughing, defecation; breath-holding spells follow crying/pain in young children

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Vasodilation/bradycardia, failed postural compensation, or low cardiac output transiently limits cerebral flow

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Initial **history, examination, orthostatic BP, ECG**; bedside glucose and targeted pregnancy/bleeding evaluation
Orthostasis: systolic fall ≥20 or diastolic ≥10 mm Hg within 3 minutes standing
High-risk → admission/monitoring; suspected structural disease → echo; intermittent arrhythmia → ambulatory ECG
Tilt-table testing for recurrent unexplained reflex/orthostatic cases; no routine head CT, EEG, carotid ultrasound
Typical breath-holding spells: normal development, awake trigger, rapid recovery; CBC/ferritin and ECG when evaluating

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Reflex event → supine, legs elevated; **hydration, counterpressure maneuvers**, trigger recognition
Orthostatic cause → replace volume, review drugs, rise slowly, compression; refractory neurogenic cases → midodrine
★ Cardiac cause → **treat rhythm/obstruction**, restrict unsafe activity pending evaluation
Breath-holding: reassure caregivers, safe positioning, treat iron deficiency; no antiseizure drugs

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, fractures, driving injury; underlying cardiac disease carries sudden-death risk
Recurrent episodes → activity limitation, anxiety; pressor drugs can cause supine hypertension

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid dehydration and prolonged immobility; individualized driving/activity restrictions after unexplained or cardiac events

rows.label: Mimics
items: Seizure: prolonged postictal confusion, lateral tongue biting
Hypoglycemia: persistent altered state until glucose corrected
TIA: focal deficit; isolated transient unconsciousness unusual

syncope.evidence: Not checked online; established syncope evaluation teaching.

trigeminal-neuralgia.name: Trigeminal neuralgia
trigeminal-neuralgia.scope: Tic douloureux, V2 and V3 lancinating facial pain, trigger zones (chewing, brushing teeth), superior cerebellar artery compression, multiple sclerosis, carbamazepine, microvascular decompression
trigeminal-neuralgia.core: Recurrent unilateral electric-shock facial pain lasting seconds, triggered by innocuous touch, most often affects the maxillary or mandibular distribution.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older adults; neurovascular compression commonly from superior cerebellar artery
Younger onset or bilateral symptoms → consider multiple sclerosis; tumor can cause secondary disease

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Chewing, toothbrushing or light facial touch** precipitates stereotyped attacks
Pain-free intervals; neurologic examination usually normal in classical disease
Objective sensory loss, bilateral symptoms, hearing findings or persistent progressive pain suggest secondary cause
Avoidance of eating and facial hygiene may result from fear of triggering pain

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Compression at root entry zone → focal demyelination and ephaptic transmission
MS-associated plaques can affect central trigeminal pathways

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical pain phenotype**; map trigeminal sensation and examine other cranial nerves
Brain MRI with trigeminal sequences evaluates neurovascular relationship, tumor and demyelination
Dental examination when uncertainty; avoid repeated irreversible dental procedures without dental pathology

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine** first-line; titrate to pain control and tolerability
Carbamazepine: CBC/LFTs/sodium, interactions; HLA-B*1502 testing with relevant Asian ancestry
Oxcarbazepine commonly causes hyponatremia; alternative/add-on baclofen or lamotrigine if needed
★ Refractory classical compression in surgical candidate → **microvascular decompression**
Poor surgical candidate → stereotactic radiosurgery or percutaneous ablative procedure; discuss sensory-loss risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Malnutrition, depression, functional restriction; drug-related rash, marrow suppression, hepatic toxicity
Ablative procedures: facial numbness, corneal injury or rare anesthesia dolorosa

rows.label: Prevention
items: No established primary prevention; maintain effective medication and monitor toxicity
Treat underlying secondary cause; counsel against abrupt unsupervised drug discontinuation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cluster headache: longer orbital attacks with prominent autonomic symptoms and restlessness
TMJ disorder: sustained ache and muscle/joint tenderness with jaw use
Postherpetic neuralgia: continuous burning pain after zoster; sensory changes

wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.name: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.scope: Wernicke encephalopathy (triad of encephalopathy, ataxia, oculomotor dysfunction), Korsakoff psychosis (confabulation, amnesia), thiamine (B1) deficiency, IV thiamine before glucose, mammillary body atrophy
wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.core: Malnourished adult with confusion, gait ataxia, or ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus; the complete Wernicke triad is often absent.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Alcohol use disorder, hyperemesis gravidarum, bariatric surgery, starvation, inadequate parenteral nutrition
Carbohydrate loading or refeeding increases thiamine demand in depleted patients

rows.label: Clues
items: Hypothermia, hypotension, or coma signal severe deficiency
★ Korsakoff: disproportionate **anterograde amnesia**, retrograde memory loss, confabulation; relatively preserved alertness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Thiamine deficiency impairs carbohydrate metabolism → ATP failure and selective neuronal injury
Medial thalami, periaqueductal gray, mammillary bodies injured → persistent amnestic syndrome

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; do not wait for vitamin assays or imaging before treatment
MRI may show symmetric thalamic/periaqueductal lesions; normal MRI does not exclude Wernicke
Chronic disease: mammillary body atrophy; evaluate glucose, electrolytes, magnesium, and competing encephalopathy causes

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected Wernicke → **high-dose IV thiamine**, followed by oral replacement after stabilization
Give thiamine before or with glucose when feasible; never delay emergency dextrose for hypoglycemia
Replete magnesium, fluid/electrolyte deficits; restore nutrition cautiously and treat alcohol withdrawal separately
Ocular findings may improve rapidly; gait/cognition recover more slowly; established amnesia often persists

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated encephalopathy → death or irreversible Korsakoff syndrome; falls and impaired independent living
Refeeding syndrome → hypophosphatemia, arrhythmias, respiratory weakness

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Routine oral **thiamine supplementation** for persistent malnutrition; nutritional assessment during alcohol treatment
Alcohol cessation support, balanced nutrition; monitor intake after bariatric surgery or prolonged vomiting

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcohol withdrawal delirium: autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, hallucinations after reduced intake
Hepatic encephalopathy: cirrhosis, asterixis, precipitating bleed or infection
Posterior circulation stroke: abrupt focal deficits; diffusion MRI identifies infarction

wernicke-korsakoff-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established thiamine-deficiency teaching.
